W_{k}

4.2.
Affine realisations

Let
\{f(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=0\}\subset A\subset\mathbb{C}^{n}
define an affine hypersurface
\{f=0\}
of an affine variety
A
. The
spinning
of
f
is the affine variety

\mathcal{S}(f)=\{(u,v,\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{C}^{2}\times A\,|\,uv=f(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\}

There is a natural projection
\mathcal{S}(f)\to A
which is a conic bundle with the zero-locus of
f
as a Morse-Bott-Lefschetz discriminant. We equip both
\{f=0\}
and
\mathcal{S}(f)
with the obvious Kähler structures induced from Euclidean space.

Lemma 4.3
.

A Lagrangian disc
D^{n}\subset\mathbb{C}^{n}
with
\partial D^{n}\subset\{f=0\}
and whose interior is disjoint from that hypersurface naturally lifts to a Lagrangian
S^{n+1}\subset\mathcal{S}(f)
.

Proof.

This ‘suspension’ (or ‘spinning’) construction is standard, see
[
58
,
2
,
24
]
. ∎

Lemma 4.4
.

W_{0}
is an affine quartic surface.

Proof.

Begin with
T^{*}S^{2}=\{xy+z^{2}=1\}=A\subset\mathbb{C}^{3}
, which has a standard Lefschetz fibration
T^{*}S^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\uppi_{z}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathbb{C}
by projection to the
z
co-ordinate, with two critical fibres. Let
f=z|_{A}
. The spinning
\mathcal{S}(f)
is then a
\mathbb{C}^{*}
-bundle over
T^{*}S^{2}
with critical fibres along a smooth conic fibre
\mathbb{C}^{*}=\uppi_{z}^{-1}(0)\subset T^{*}S^{2}
. The zero-section
S^{2}
which is a matching sphere for the path
[-1,1]\subset\mathbb{C}_{z}
meets the critical fibre in a circle, and each of its two constituent discs spin to a Lagrangian
3
-sphere. These two spheres meet cleanly along the unknotted circle
\mathbb{C}_{z}\cap S^{2}
. The Morse-Bott surgery of the two 3-spheres is the
S^{1}\times S^{2}
obtained from spinning up a perturbation of the zero-section in
T^{*}S^{2}
which does not meet the critical fibre. It follows that the total space is the completion of a subdomain symplectomorphic to
W_{0}
. The total space
\mathcal{S}(f)
is defined by
\{xy+u^{2}v^{2}=1\}\subset\mathbb{C}^{4}
, which is an affine quartic.
∎

The variety
F
of complete flags in
\mathbb{C}^{3}
is a smooth hypersurface in
\mathbb{P}^{2}\times\mathbb{P}^{2}
of bidegree
(1,1)
.

Lemma 4.5
.

W_{1}
is an affine flag 3-fold.

Proof.

Fix
F=\{xx^{\prime}+yy^{\prime}+zz^{\prime}=0\}\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}\times\mathbb{P}^{2}
and consider the map
(\mathbb{P}^{2}\times\mathbb{P}^{2})\backslash\Theta\to\mathbb{P}^{2}
given by

([x:y:z]),([x^{\prime}:y^{\prime}:z^{\prime}])\mapsto[xx^{\prime}:yy^{\prime}:zz^{\prime}]

which is defined away from the hexagon of lines
\Theta=\{xx^{\prime}=yy^{\prime}=zz^{\prime}=0\}\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}\times\mathbb{P}^{2}
. We pull back a pencil of lines on
\mathbb{P}^{2}
, and consider the pencil of
(1,1)
-divisors

D_{[\uplambda:\upmu]}=\{\uplambda(xx^{\prime}-zz^{\prime})+\upmu\,yy^{\prime}=0\}\cap F\,\subset F,\qquad[\uplambda:\upmu]\in\mathbb{P}^{1},

again with base locus
\Theta
. Remove the smooth fibre
D_{[1:0]}\cap F
from
F
, which is a del Pezzo surface of degree six representing
-K_{F}/2
. The projection
p=\uplambda/\upmu\colon F\backslash D_{[1:0]}\to\mathbb{C}
is then a Morse-Bott-Lefschetz fibration with general fibre
(\mathbb{C}^{*})^{2}
as in Example
4.2
, and with singular fibres over
\{0,\pm 1\}
. The map
p
is equivariant for a Hamiltonian
T^{2}
-action

(\upvartheta,\upphi)\cdot([x:y:z],[x^{\prime}:y^{\prime}:z^{\prime}])\ =\ ([e^{i\upvartheta}x:y:e^{i\upphi}z],[e^{-i\upvartheta}x^{\prime}:y^{\prime}:e^{-i\upphi}z^{\prime}])

on
\mathbb{P}^{2}\times\mathbb{P}^{2}
, which has proper moment map restricted to
W_{1}
. There are two Lagrangian 3-spheres which fibre, as Morse-Bott matching cycles, over the arcs
[-1,0]
and
[0,1]\subset\mathbb{C}
. The circles which collapse at the critical fibres are those corresponding to
\upvartheta=0
respectively
\upphi=0
at
\pm 1
, and
\upvartheta=\upphi
at
0
. This shows that the two 3-spheres meet according to the
W_{1}
-plumbing. ∎

Remark 4.6
.

Jonny Evans (private communication) has shown that the union of the two matching spheres form a Lagrangian skeleton of
W_{1}
, i.e. they are the critical locus of a global plurisubharmonic function. The weaker fact that
W_{1}
embeds into the flag 3-fold follows from ‘semi-toric’ considerations, cf.
[
43
, Figure 10(b)]
. This exhibits a singular Lagrangian torus fibration on
F
in which two 3-spheres meeting cleanly along a circle are mapped to straight arcs in the base of the fibration (the ‘moment polytope’). By considering the slopes of those arcs in the affine structure in the base, one sees that the local model is that of
W_{1}
.

Remark 4.7
.

We do not know if
W_{n}
is affine if
n>1
, but Remark
3.14
shows that
W_{n}
embeds as a Stein subdomain of an affine variety.
W_{1}
is a smoothing of the cone
\mathrm{Cone}(-K_{S})
given by collapsing the zero-section in the anticanonical bundle over a del Pezzo surface
S
diffeomorphic to the 3-point blow-up of
\mathbb{C}P^{2}
. A smoothing of
\mathrm{Cone}(-K_{S}^{\otimes n})
gives an affine model for a plumbing of two Lens spaces.

Remark 4.8
.

\mathbb{P}^{3}
contains no Lagrangian sphere
[
56
]
, whilst a quadric 3-fold cannot contain two Lagrangian 3-spheres meeting cleanly along a circle (an easy consequence of results in
[
63
]
). Degeneration techniques show a hypersurface
H_{d}\subset\mathbb{P}^{4}
of degree
d\geqslant 4
, or a complete intersection
H_{d,d^{\prime}}\subset\mathbb{P}^{5}
of bidegrees
d,d^{\prime}\geqslant 2
, contains two Lagrangian 3-spheres meeting cleanly in a circle.

4.3.
A digression on knotting

The realisation of
W_{0}
as an affine quartic yields an attractive local obstruction to knotting. Recall that a
dilation
on a Stein manifold
Y
is a class
b\in SH^{1}(Y)
in the first symplectic cohomology with
\Delta(b)=1
, where
\Delta
is the
BV
-operator. If
Y
admits a dilation, it admits no exact Lagrangian
K(\uppi,1)
by
[
59
]
.

Lemma 4.9
.

W_{0}
admits a dilation.

Proof.

We will construct an embedding of
W_{0}
into the total space of a Lefschetz fibration over
\mathbb{C}
with fibre the
A_{3}
-Milnor fibre. The result will then follow from
[
59
, Proposition 7.3]
together with Viterbo restriction (which takes dilations to dilations).

Inside the four-real-dimensional
A_{3}
-Milnor fibre
M
we can find two Lagrangian matching 2-spheres which meet cleanly along a circle: if the critical points of the standard Lefschetz fibration
M\to\mathcal{C}
lie at
\{1,2,3,4\}\subset\mathcal{C}
and the obvious real matching spheres are labelled
S_{1},S_{2},S_{3}
then we can take the spheres
S_{1}
and
S^{\prime}=\uptau_{S_{2}}^{2}(S_{3})
. We now construct
Z
as the total space of a Lefschetz fibration with four singular fibres at
\{i,2i,3i,4i\}\subset\mathcal{C}
, for which the associated vanishing cycles along paths parallel to
\mathbb{R}_{\geqslant 0}
are respectively
S_{1},S_{1},S^{\prime},S^{\prime\prime}
, where
S^{\prime\prime}
is chosen so that when the basis of vanishing paths is mutated so as to replace the fourth one with a path passing through
3i/2
then the corresponding vanishing cycle agrees with
S^{\prime}
. In this total space, the interval
[i,2i]\subset i\mathbb{R}
is a matching path, as is a path from
3i
to
4i
which meets the interval
[i,2i]
in its interior transversely once. The corresponding spheres in the
A_{3}
-fibre are identified with
S_{1}
and
S^{\prime}
. In particular, this constructs a pair of Lagrangian 3-spheres in
Z
which meet cleanly along a circle, hence an embedding of some double bubble
W_{k}
into
Z
. It remains to identify
k
.

The
A_{3}
Milnor fibre admits a circle action compatible with its Lefschetz fibration structure over
\mathbb{C}
; the spheres
S_{i}
and
S^{\prime}
are setwise
S^{1}
-invariant and meet along an orbit. Since this action is compatible with the
Br_{4}
-action on the Milnor fibre, there is an induced fibrewise action on
Z
, and the 3-dimensional matching spheres in
Z
again meet along an orbit. One can then construct the surgery of the two matching spheres equivariantly to obtain a 3-manifold
K
which carries an induced
S^{1}
-action free in a neighbourhood of the surgery locus. Inspection shows that globally the action has no exceptional orbits (with non-trivial finite stabiliser) and two circles of fixed points (coming from points lying at the endpoints of the matching spheres in the
A_{3}
-fibres, over the intervals of points comprising the matching paths in the base of
Z\to\mathbb{C}
); moreover the quotient of the action has genus zero and is orientable. It follows that the surgery
K
is diffeomorphic to
S^{1}\times S^{2}
from the classification of circle actions on 3-manifolds with non-empty fixed point loci
[
54
, Theorem 1, (ii)a]
. We conclude that a neighbourhood in
Z
of the embedded double bubble plumbing is symplectomorphic to
W_{0}
.
∎

Proposition 4.10
.

There is no Hamiltonian isotopy of the spheres
Q_{i}\subset W_{0}
to a pair of spheres meeting cleanly in a circle knotted in either component.

Proof.

Suppose such an isotopy exists, yielding an embedding
W_{n}(\upkappa_{1},\upkappa_{2})\subset W_{0}
with at least one
\upkappa_{i}
non-trivial. Label the core spheres of the knotted clean intersection
Q_{i}^{\prime}
. Since the
Q_{i}^{\prime}
are isomorphic in the Fukaya category to the
Q_{i}
, necessarily
n=0
from (
2.3
). By compatibility of the unit and BV-operator with Viterbo restriction, we see that
W_{0}(\upkappa_{1},\upkappa_{2})
also admits a dilation, hence contains no exact Lagrangian
K(\uppi,1)
. If
\upkappa_{2}
is the trivial knot, then the Bott surgery
K
of the isotoped spheres
Q_{i}^{\prime}
is given by
0
-surgery on
\upkappa_{1}
. If
\upkappa_{1}
is non-trivial, this is aspherical by Gabai’s proof of Property
R

[
21
]
, a contradiction. So we can suppose both
\upkappa_{i}
are non-trivial. Then the surgery admits an incompressible torus.

By a result of Ganatra-Pomerleano
[
24
, Corollary 5.9]
, again building on
[
42
]
, one sees that the surgery
K
of the
Q_{i}^{\prime}
– whose cotangent bundle also admits a dilation, by the same restriction argument, and hence a quasi-dilation – is finitely covered by
S^{1}\times\Sigma_{g}
(
g\geqslant 1
) or by a connect sum of
S^{1}\times S^{2}
’s. In the former case,
K
is aspherical, which is a contradiction. Thus
K
is finitely covered by
\#_{k}(S^{1}\times S^{2})
for some
k\geqslant 0
. These are exactly the manifolds with no aspherical summand in their prime decomposition; since
H_{1}(K;\mathbb{Q})\cong\mathbb{Q}
, we see that
K=(S^{1}\times S^{2})\#M
for
M
a connect sum of spherical 3-manifolds. But this means
\uppi_{1}(K)
is a free product of
\mathbb{Z}
and a collection of finite groups, and this contains no
\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}
subgroup by Kurosh’s theorem, contradicting existence of the incompressible torus.
∎

We remark that there is no smooth obstruction to changing the knot type of the intersection.

After the first version of this note was circulated, Ganatra and Pomerleano constructed a quasi-dilation on
W_{1}
in characteristic 3, which extends
1
1

1

The first version of this note used
ad hoc
methods to prove a weaker result, namely that the only possible non-trivial knot type that could occur in
W_{1}
was the trefoil.
Proposition
4.10
from
W_{0}
to
W_{1}
. When
p>1
is prime, one can rule out some knot types using the classification result Corollary
6.13
, along the vein of the topological Corollaries given in the Introduction.

4.4.
Monodromy

A Lagrangian sphere
L\subset X
has an associated Dehn twist symplectomorphism
\uptau_{L}
. Keating
[
37
]
proved that the Dehn twists
\uptau_{Q_{1}}
and
\uptau_{Q_{2}}
generate a free group inside the mapping class group
\uppi_{0}\,\mathrm{Symp}_{ct}(W_{\upeta}(\upkappa_{1},\upkappa_{2}))
. Since the intersection pairing on
H_{3}(W_{n}(\upkappa_{1},\upkappa_{2});\mathbb{Z})
is trivial, the twists
\uptau_{Q_{i}}
act trivially on cohomology. The cone
K=\{Q_{1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle e}}{{\longrightarrow}}Q_{2}\}
has surgery representative a Lagrangian Lens space, hence there is a geometric Dehn twist
\uptau_{K}
(cf.
[
50
]
for the Lens space case). The Lens space
K
represents the diagonal homology class in

H_{3}(W_{n};\mathbb{Z}/2)\,\cong\,\mathbb{Z}/2\langle Q_{1}\rangle\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2\langle Q_{2}\rangle

so (even when
n=1
and
K
is a sphere)
K
is not quasi-isomorphic in
\mathcal{F}(W_{n})
to the image of
Q_{i}
under any element of
\langle\uptau_{Q_{1}},\uptau_{Q_{2}}\rangle
, and
\uptau_{K}
does not belong to this group. The question arises as to which larger group naturally acts, i.e. what is the group
\langle\uptau_{Q_{1}},\uptau_{Q_{2}},\uptau_{K}\rangle
.

Let
\mathrm{Br}_{3}=\langle a,b\,|\,aba=bab\rangle
denote the braid group on 3 strings. The kernel of the natural surjection
\mathrm{Br}_{3}\to\mathrm{Sym}_{3}
, which quotients out the subgroup normally generated by
a^{2}
and
b^{2}
, is called the
pure braid group

\mathrm{PBr}_{3}
. One can also consider the preimage of a subgroup
S_{2}\leqslant S_{3}
, to define the
mixed braid group

\mathrm{MBr}_{3}
of braids which fix one end-point. The pure braid group
\mathrm{PBr}_{3}
is generated by either of the triples
\{a^{2},b^{2},ab^{2}a^{-1}\}
or
\{a^{2},b^{2},(aba)^{2}\}
, the mixed braid group
\mathrm{MBr}_{3}
by
\{a^{2},b^{2},(aba)\}
.

Lemma 4.11
.

There is a natural representation
\uprho_{0}\colon\mathrm{MBr}_{3}\to\uppi_{0}\,\mathrm{Symp}(W_{0})
.

Proof.

The construction of the affine quartic above has input (i) an element of
\mathrm{Conf}_{2}(\mathbb{C})
, defining a degree two polynomial
p(z)
with distinct roots and hence an affine surface
S_{p}=\{xy+p(z)=0\}
symplectically equivalent to
T^{*}S^{2}
; and a point
\uplambda\in\mathbb{C}\backslash\{p^{-1}(0)\}
defining a smooth conic fibre of the projection
S_{p}\to\mathbb{C}_{z}
about which one can spin to produce the 3-fold. One therefore obtains a family of affine quartics over a bundle over
\mathrm{Conf}_{2}(\mathbb{C})\simeq S^{1}
with fibre a twice-punctured plane. This parameter space has fundamental group
\mathrm{MBr}_{3}
. The representation is then obtained from symplectic parallel transport, well-defined since one can work relative to a family of compactification divisors with fixed topology.

The generator
a^{2}
of
\mathrm{MBr}_{3}
is represented by the monodromy of a loop of affine varieties in which one of the Lefschetz critical points of
T^{*}S^{2}\to\mathbb{C}
rotates around the fixed fibre in which we spin to construct the threefold. One can therefore view this as the monodromy of a family of varieties over a disc, in which the central fibre is singular, obtained by spinning
\{uv=\uppi\}
along a
singular
conic fibre, so where
\uppi^{-1}(0)
is a critical fibre of the Lefschetz fibration
\uppi\colon T^{*}S^{2}\to\mathbb{C}
. The family of threefolds then acquires a nodal singularity
\{uv=x^{2}+y^{2}\}
, so the monodromy is isotopic to the Dehn twist in the corresponding vanishing cycle. It follows that
\uprho_{0}
takes
\{a^{2},b^{2}\}
to the Dehn twists
\{\uptau_{Q_{1}},\uptau_{Q_{2}}\}
.

The generator
(aba)
of
\mathrm{MBr}_{3}
is a lift, under the map
\mathrm{MBr}_{3}\to\mathrm{Br}_{2}
which forgets the fixed strand, of the generating half-twist exchanging the other two strands. Since the fixed strand corresponds to the location of the fibre over which we spin, this means that it is a lift to
W_{0}
of the Dehn twist in the zero-section of
T^{*}S^{2}
, under the natural map
W_{0}\to T^{*}S^{2}
.
∎

Remark 4.12
.

If
L=S^{1}\times S^{2}\subset X
is a Lagrangian
S^{1}\times S^{2}
, the non-compactly-supported symplectomorphism
\mathrm{id}\times\uptau_{S^{2}}\in\mathrm{Symp}(T^{*}S^{1}\times T^{*}S^{2})
need not extend to a global symplectomorphism of
X
; our situation is special since
W_{0}
admits a global map to
T^{*}S^{2}
. This phenomenon is familiar on the B-side of the mirror, where there are objects
\mathcal{E}
such that

\mathrm{Hom}^{*}(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{E})=\begin{cases}k[x]&*\in\{0,2\}\\
0&else.\end{cases}

The existence of an associated autoequivalence is again delicate, because the object
\mathcal{E}
defining the autoequivalence admits an
infinite
filtration by copies of the underlying
(S^{1}\times S^{2})
-type-object
E
, hence need not belong to the ‘compact’ category in question.

Consider a Morse-Bott-Lefschetz fibration
T^{*}S^{3}\cong E_{1}
as in Example
4.2
, with singular fibres at
\{0,1\}
with vanishing cycles the usual meridional and longitude curves on the torus (call these
a
and
b
say). One can construct a family of Morse-Bott-Lefschetz fibrations
E_{\uplambda}
over
\mathbb{C}^{*}
with singular fibres at
0
and
\uplambda
, and there is a monodromy symplectomorphism
\upphi_{1}\colon E_{1}\to E_{1}
associated to parallel transport around the unit circle.

Lemma 4.13
.

The symplectomorphism
\upphi_{1}\colon E_{1}\to E_{1}
is the Dehn twist.

Proof.

We adapt a construction from
[
64
]
, see also
[
28
]
. Consider a Morse-Bott-Lefschetz fibration with general fibre
(\mathbb{C}^{*})^{2}
, with two critical fibres
(\mathbb{C}^{*})\times(\mathbb{C}\vee\mathbb{C})
, and with total space containing a matching 3-sphere fibred over an arc between the critical values. Such a fibration can be obtained as the fibre product of a pair of two-complex-dimensional Lefschetz fibrations
\uppi_{i}\colon X_{i}\to\mathbb{C}
with general fibre
\mathbb{C}^{*}
, each with a single singular fibre
\mathbb{C}\vee\mathbb{C}
, and whose critical values do not agree. The half-twist exchanging the critical values is realised by monodromy around a family in which the singular fibre is the self-fibre product

\{(u,v,x,y)\in\mathbb{C}^{2}\times\mathbb{C}^{2}\,|\,\uppi(u,v)=\uppi(x,y)\}

of the standard Lefschetz singularity
\uppi\colon\mathbb{C}^{2}\to\mathbb{C}
,
\uppi(u,v)=u^{2}+v^{2}
. This is again a threefold ordinary double point.
∎

This local model admits fibrewise
\mathbb{Z}/k
-actions which give a corresponding description for the cotangent bundle of a Lens space, and a similar monodromy viewpoint on the Lens space Dehn twist.
Viewing
T^{*}S^{3}=\{z_{0}z_{1}+z_{2}z_{3}=1\}\subset\mathbb{C}^{4}
, the Morse-Bott-Lefschetz fibration is given by projection to
z_{0}z_{1}
, and there is a fibrewise Hamiltonian action of
T^{2}
generated by circle actions with weights
(1,-1,0,0)
and
(0,0,1,-1)
. The
\mathbb{Z}/k
diagonal subgroup acts freely and has quotient
T^{*}(L(k,1))
. Viewing the original
T^{2}
as generated by the first and diagonal circle actions (so the vanishing cycles degenerating at the two Morse-Bott critical points are
a
and
b-a
), there is a moment map

(z_{0},\ldots,z_{3})\ \mapsto\ (|z_{0}|^{2}-|z_{1}|^{2},|z_{0}|^{2}-|z_{1}|^{2}+|z_{2}|^{2}-|z_{3}|^{2})

The
T^{2}
action descends to the quotient with moment map

(z_{0},\ldots,z_{3})\ \mapsto\ (|z_{0}|^{2}-|z_{1}|^{2},(|z_{0}|^{2}-|z_{1}|^{2}+|z_{2}|^{2}-|z_{3}|^{2})/k)

and with vanishing cycles
a,kb-a
(cf. Example
4.2
). Let
E_{k}
denote this quotient fibration; there is again a symplectomorphism

\upphi_{k}\colon E_{k}\to E_{k}

from parallel transport around the unit circle for the family of fibrations with critical fibres at
0
and
\uplambda\in\mathbb{C}^{*}
.

Lemma 4.14
.

The full twist monodromy
\upphi_{k}\colon E_{k}\to E_{k}
is Hamiltonian isotopic to the Lens space Dehn twist.

Proof.

The
\mathbb{Z}/k
-action discussed above exists in the total space of the family considered in Lemma
4.13
. By construction, there is therefore a commuting diagram

\textstyle{T^{*}S^{3}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\upphi_{1}}
\textstyle{T^{*}S^{3}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\textstyle{T^{*}L(k,1)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\scriptstyle{\upphi_{k}}
\textstyle{T^{*}L(k,1)}

with vertical maps the
\mathbb{Z}/k
quotients introduced previously.
Since
\upphi_{1}
is the spherical twist,
\upphi_{k}
is the Lens space twist up to composition with a deck transformation; but both monodromies are compactly supported.
∎

Lemma 4.15
.

For
k\geqslant 1
, there is a natural representation
\uprho_{k}\colon\mathrm{PBr}_{3}\to\uppi_{0}\,\mathrm{Symp}(W_{k})
, whose image is generated by (spherical and Lens space) Dehn twists in the core components and their surgery.

Proof.

As in Lemma
4.11
, we obtain the representation
\uprho_{k}
from parallel transport, now via the geometry of families of Morse-Bott-Lefschetz fibrations as in the set-up for Lemma
4.13
but for fibrations with three critical fibres. This immediately shows, when
k=1
, for the representation
\uprho_{1}
the generating half-twists
a^{2},b^{2},ab^{2}a^{-1}
correspond to Dehn twists in
Q_{1},Q_{2},K
, viewed as monodromies of global degenerations. For higher
k
, an appeal to Lemma
4.14
shows that two of the pure braid group generators which perform a full twist in a pair of generators are taken to spherical twists in the cores, whilst the ‘third’ pure braid group generator acts as the Lens space twist.
∎

Remark 4.16
.

For
k\geqslant 1
, each element of the image of
\uprho_{k}
is isotopic to a compactly supported symplectomorphism (this is not true when
k=0
).
When
k=1
, the monodromy can also be understood via transport in families of affine flag 3-folds as in Lemma
4.5
. From that viewpoint, it is clear that the whole representation
\uprho_{1}
lifts to
\uppi_{0}\,\mathrm{Symp}_{ct}(W_{1})
.

Remark 4.17
.

Lemma
4.5
shows that the contact boundary of
W_{1}
admits a free contact circle action, since it is the circle bundle over a smooth del Pezzo surface. If
(Y,\upxi)
is a contact manifold carrying a contact circle action, there is an associated compactly supported symplectomorphism of the symplectization (by suspending the action), which here gives rise to a symplectomorphism
\uptau_{\partial}\in\uppi_{0}\,\mathrm{Symp}_{ct}(W_{1})
which is a “boundary twist”. The monodromy
\uprho_{1}
takes
(aba)^{2}
, which generates the centre of
\mathrm{PBr}_{3}
, to the boundary twist
\uptau_{\partial}
. This follows by considering a Lefschetz pencil of
(1,1)
-divisors in
\mathbb{P}^{2}\times\mathbb{P}^{2}
over
\mathbb{P}^{1}
, with 3 critical fibres; the global monodromy rotates the normal bundle of the base locus.

4.5.
A-side Twists

The Dehn twist in an exact Lagrangian sphere
L\cong S^{3}\subset X
acts by a twist functor on the Fukaya category:

(4.1)

\uptau_{L}\simeq\mathrm{Cone}\,(\hom_{\mathcal{F}(X)}(L,\bullet)\otimes L\stackrel{{\scriptstyle ev}}{{\longrightarrow}}\bullet)

where (
4.1
) denotes an isomorphism in the category
nu
-
fun(\mathcal{F}(X),\mathcal{F}(X))
of non-unital
A_{\infty}
-functors of
\mathcal{F}(X)
, see
[
57
]
. The action of a Lens space Dehn twist on the Fukaya category was analysed by Mak and Wu
[
50
]
. They prove that if
L\cong L(p,1)\subset X
is an exact Lagrangian Lens space and one works over a field
\mathbb{K}
of characteristic
p
, then for any other exact Lagrangian
K\subset X
there is a quasi-isomorphism

(4.2)

\uptau_{L}(K)\simeq\mathrm{Cone}\,(\hom_{\mathcal{F}(X)}(\mathcal{L},K)\otimes_{\mathbb{K}[\uppi_{1}(L)]}\mathcal{L}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle ev}}{{\longrightarrow}}K)

where
\mathcal{L}
denotes the universal local system over
L
and
ev
is now a suitable equivariant evaluation map, see
[
50
]
for details. We briefly recall that, fixing an isomorphism
\uppi_{1}(L)=\mathbb{Z}/p
, there is an isomorphism of
\mathbb{K}[\uppi_{1}(L)]
-modules

\hom_{\mathcal{F}}^{*}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L})=(C^{*}(\widehat{L})\otimes\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{K}}(\mathbb{K}[\mathbb{Z}/p],\mathbb{K}[\mathbb{Z}/p]))^{\mathbb{Z}/p}

where
S^{3}=\widehat{L}\to L
is the universal cover, and we also note that
[
50
, Lemma 2.13]
gives an isomorphism of
\mathbb{K}
-algebras

(4.3)

HF^{*}(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{L})=H^{*}(S^{3})\otimes_{\mathbb{K}}\mathbb{K}[\uppi_{1}(L)].

Remark 4.18
.

It is presumably true, but not yet known, that (
4.2
) again arises from an exact triangle of functors.

The
A_{\infty}
-endomorphism algebra of an object
E
in a
3
-CY category gives rise to a noncommutative deformation functor, and hence a universal object
\mathcal{E}
. We say that
E
is fat-spherical if
\mathrm{Hom}^{i}(\mathcal{E},E)
is the cohomology of a sphere
[
65
]
. The dimension of this sphere can vary; in Remark
4.12
the fat-spherical object is the 2-sphere, whilst below for flopping contractions only the 3-sphere will turn out to be possible.

Below it will be a feature of our categories
\mathcal{C}_{k}
that the universal objects
\mathcal{E}
of our fat spherical objects will always turn out to satisfy

(4.4)

\mathrm{Hom}^{i}(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{E})=\begin{cases}\mathbb{K}[x]/(x^{n})&i=0,3\\
0&\mathrm{else},\end{cases}

and indeed such an
\mathcal{E}
will be mirror to the universal local system
\mathcal{L}
of (
4.3
) (the universal object
\mathcal{E}
respectively
\mathcal{L}
arises via the same iterated mapping cone on
E
respectively
L
). The usual association of autoequivalences to spherical objects carries over to the fat-spherical case: any fat-spherical object (or more precisely, its corresponding universal object) determines an autoequivalence, by e.g.
[
65
]
.

If
\mathrm{char}\,\mathbb{K}=0
, then the Lens space
L(p,1)
supports
p
distinct rank one local systems associated to the unitary characters of
\uppi_{1}(L)
; each of these determines a spherical object
S_{i}\in\mathcal{F}(X;\mathbb{K})
. These spherical objects are pairwise orthogonal, and so their associated twists commute.
[
50
]
implies that

•

when
\mathrm{char}(\mathbb{K})=p
, the Lens space twist acts on objects of the Fukaya category by the fat spherical twist associated to the object
\mathcal{L}
;

•

when
\mathrm{char}(\mathbb{K})=0
, the Lens space twist acts on objects of
\mathcal{F}(X)
as the product of spherical twists
T_{S_{1}}\ldots T_{S_{p}}
.

4.6.
Generation

If
\mathcal{D}\subset\mathcal{F}(X)
is a full subcategory, we say
\mathcal{D}
split-generates if every object of
\mathrm{D}^{\uppi}\,\mathcal{F}(X)
is quasi-equivalent to an object of
\mathrm{D}^{\uppi}\,\mathcal{D}
. Let
\mathcal{Q}_{n}
denote the full subcategory of
\mathrm{D}^{\uppi}\,\mathcal{F}(W_{n})
split-generated by the two core spheres
Q_{1}
and
Q_{2}
.

Lemma 4.19
.

Let
n=0
. The core spheres
\{Q_{i}\}
do not split-generate
\mathcal{F}(W_{n})
.

Proof.

Consider the Morse-Bott surgery
K=\{Q_{1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\upkappa}}{{\longrightarrow}}Q_{2}\}
, diffeomorphic to
S^{1}\times S^{2}
. Let
\upxi\to K
be a rank one local system with non-trivial monodromy; this defines a Lagrangian brane
\upxi\to K
which is an object of
\mathcal{F}(W_{0})
. The endomorphisms of this object are given by

HF^{*}((\upxi\to K),(\upxi\to K))\cong H^{*}(K,\mathrm{End}(\upxi))\cong H^{*}(K)

so
\upxi\to K
is a non-zero object. From the description of
W_{n}
in terms of a
(\mathbb{C}^{*})^{2}
-Morse-Bott-Lefschetz fibration in Example
4.2
, one sees that one can construct the surgery
K
so that there are clean intersections
K\cap Q_{i}\cong S^{1}
for each
i
, where moreover the
S^{1}
is a homology generator for
H_{1}(K;\mathbb{Z})
. The Floer cohomology

HF^{*}(Q_{i},(\upxi\to K))\cong H^{*}(S^{1},\upxi)

which vanishes for non-trivial
\upxi
. We have therefore produced a non-trivial object of
\mathcal{F}(W_{0})
which is orthogonal to both the
Q_{i}
.
∎

When
n>1
, the same proof goes through over
\mathbb{C}
: the cone
K
is a Lens space which is split-generated by the
Q_{i}
when equipped with the trivial local system, but not when equipped with a local system associated to a non-trivial character of
\mathbb{Z}/n
.

Lemma 4.20
.

Let
n=1
. The core spheres
\{Q_{i}\}
split-generate
\mathcal{F}(W_{1})
.

Proof.

This follows from Remark
4.17
and
[
57
, Corollary 5.8]
; a “boundary twist”, which acts on
\mathcal{F}(W_{1})
by a non-trivial shift, can be expressed in terms of Dehn twists in spheres generated by
\mathcal{Q}_{1}
(compare to Remark
4.17
). For a Lefschetz pencil of hypersurfaces
\{D_{t}\}\subset Z
on a projective variety cut out by sections of a line bundle
\mathcal{L}\to Z
with
\mathcal{L}^{\otimes-d}=K_{Z}
, the shift associated to the global monodromy on the affine part
D_{0}\backslash(D_{0}\cap D_{\infty})
is
4-2d
, cf.
[
57
, Section 19b]
. In our case, we have a pencil of
(1,1)
-divisors in
\mathbb{P}^{2}\times\mathbb{P}^{2}
so
d=3
.
∎

We now give a version of Lemma
4.20
which does not rely on having an affine model for
W_{k}
when
k\neq\{0,1\}
.

Let
\mathcal{W}(\mathcal{W}_{k};\mathbb{K})
denote the wrapped Fukaya category of the Stein manifold
W_{k}
, defined over the field
\mathbb{K}
. The wrapped category is invariant under not necessarily compactly supported Hamiltonian isotopies, so there is a representation

(4.5)

\uppi_{0}\,\mathrm{Symp}(W_{k})\longrightarrow\operatorname{Auteq}(\mathcal{W}(W_{k};\mathbb{K}))/\langle[2]\rangle

into the quotient of the autoequivalence group by twice the shift. This lifts to a representation of the central
\mathbb{Z}
-extension
\uppi_{0}\,\mathrm{Symp}_{gr}(W_{k})
of isotopy classes of graded symplectomorphisms into
\operatorname{Auteq}(\mathcal{W}_{k};\mathbb{K})
. The following result should be compared to Remark
4.17
.

Lemma 4.21
.

Suppose
k=1
and
\mathrm{char}\,\mathbb{K}=0
or
k>2
is prime and
\mathbb{K}
has characteristic
k
.
The centre of the pure braid group
\mathrm{PBr}_{3}
acts on
\mathcal{W}(W_{k};\mathbb{K})
by a non-trivial negative shift.

Proof.

Working with not necessarily compactly supported representatives coming from parallel transport, the central element of the braid group is represented by the ‘boundary twist’ in
\mathrm{PBr}_{3}\simeq\uppi_{0}\,\mathrm{Diff}(D^{2};\{p,q,r\})
. Thus
\uprho
is geometrically a lift to the total space of the Morse-Bott-Lefschetz fibration
W_{k}
of the Dehn twist near infinity in the base; undoing that Dehn twist by an isotopy which rotates infinity clockwise shows that
\uprho
is trivial in
\uppi_{0}\,\mathrm{Symp}(W_{k})
. Then (
4.5
) shows that it acts on the wrapped category by an even shift. The value of the shift can then be checked on any object. When
k=1
, we know the shift is
[-2]
by Lemma
4.20
. Away from
k=1
, we argue that the shift is still
[-2]
as follows.

Following the convention from
[
56
]
, the Dehn twist in a Lagrangian sphere has a canonical lift to a graded symplectomorphism
2
2

2

Gradings in
(X,\omega)
are determined by a choice of infinite cyclic cover of the Lagrangian Grassmannian bundle of
TX
which is fibrewise universal, and the canonical graded lift is uniquely determined by acting trivially on the fibres of this cover near infinity in
X
.
; the same is true for a Lens space twist. We will continue to write
\uptau_{L}
for this canonical graded lift. In both cases, the canonical lift shifts the object itself by
[-2]
, cf.
[
56
, Lemma 5.7]
. We have fixed gradings on the core spheres
Q_{1}
and
Q_{2}
so that

(4.6)

HF^{*}(Q_{1},Q_{2})=H^{*}(S^{1})[-1]=HF^{*}(Q_{2},Q_{1})

are both concentrated in degrees
1
and
2
. Furthermore, we know from the discussion around (
2.2
) that the Lagrange surgeries
K=K_{1}
(fibred over an arc in the upper half-plane in the Morse-Bott-Lefschetz model) and
K^{\prime}=K_{2}
(fibred over an arc in the lower half-plane) are canonically graded by their presentation as Bott surgeries, with phase functions which extend those on the
Q_{i}
. The analogue of
[
56
, Lemma 5.8]
in this context, with exactly the same proof, is then that there are isotopies

(4.7)

\uptau_{Q_{1}}(K_{2})=K_{1}\qquad\uptau_{Q_{2}}(K_{1})=K_{2}

as
graded
Lagrangians. Note that our situation is more symmetric than the general case treated by Seidel in
op. cit.
because of the grading symmetry in (
4.6
).

With
s_{1}
and
s_{2}
being the usual generators of the braid group, we have

\uptau_{Q_{1}}=s_{1}^{2},\ \uptau_{Q_{2}}=s_{2}^{2},\ \uptau_{K_{2}}=s_{2}s_{1}^{2}s_{2}^{-1}

(the third being the Lens space twist in the
K_{2}
-surgery). The centre
\uprho
of the pure braid group is given by

\uprho=\uptau_{Q_{1}}\circ\uptau_{K_{2}}\circ\uptau_{Q_{2}}

where we have broken symmetry by ordering
Q_{1}
and
Q_{2}
which accounts for the appearance of a choice of surgery in the middle. We compute the shift by applying this to the object
A=\uptau_{Q_{2}}^{-1}(K_{2})
; this is mapped to
\uptau_{Q_{1}}(K_{2}[-2])
, using that
\uptau_{K_{2}}(K_{2})=K_{2}[-2]
as commented above. On the other hand, we already know this image must be some even shift
A[2k]
of
A
itself. To prove
k=-1
it remains to show that
\uptau_{Q_{1}}(K_{2}[-2])=\uptau_{Q_{2}}^{-1}(K_{2})[-2]
, or equivalently that
\uptau_{Q_{2}}\uptau_{Q_{1}}(K_{2})=K_{2}
, which follows from (
4.7
).
∎

Corollary 4.22
.

Let
k>2
be prime and suppose
\mathrm{char}\,\mathbb{K}=k
. Then the core spheres
Q_{i}
split-generate the compact category
\mathcal{F}(W_{k};\mathbb{K})
.

Proof.

Whenever a composition of (fat) spherical twists acts by a shift, the corresponding objects split-generate, compare to
[
57
]
. This means the core spheres together with the fat-spherical object (whose universal object is)
\mathcal{L}
underlying the Lens space twist split-generate. In characteristic
k
, the Lens space
L=L(k,1)
has a non-trivial class
\upeta\in HF^{1}(L,L)=\mathbb{K}
and hence a graded self-extension
L\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\upeta}}{{\longrightarrow}}L
. When
k=2
, this represents the universal local system
\mathcal{L}
associated to
L
. More generally, the universal local system
\mathcal{L}
over
L
has endomorphisms as in (
4.4
); it determines the underlying fat-spherical object
L
of the associated autoequivalence, and the general theory of fat-spherical objects (see e.g.
[
36
,
50
]
) implies that
\mathcal{L}
is filtered by copies of
L
. Therefore the core spheres together with
L
split-generate. But the Lens space itself is manifestly generated by the cores.
∎

Remark 4.23
.

When
k>2
and
\mathrm{char}\,\mathbb{K}=0
the same argument and the description of the Lens space twist at the end of Section
4.5
shows that
\mathcal{F}(W_{k})
is split-generated by the cores
Q_{i}
and the collection of branes given by equipping the Lens space with a non-trivial rank one local system.

Remark 4.24
.

If
k>1
, then the Lens space Dehn twist
\uptau_{L}\in\uppi_{0}\,\mathrm{Symp}_{ct}(W_{k})
acts on
\mathcal{F}(W_{k};\mathbb{C})
by a product of spherical twists. However, the individual twist equivalences
T_{S_{i}}\in\operatorname{Auteq}(\mathcal{F}(W_{k};\mathbb{C}))
have no obvious geometric origin, i.e. they are not visibly in the image of
\uppi_{0}\,\mathrm{Symp}_{ct}(W_{k})
.

Remark 4.25
.

Proposition
2.9
gives an equivalence over
\mathbb{C}

\mathcal{Q}_{1}\simeq\mathcal{Q}_{k}\qquad k\geqslant 2

However, this is
not

\mathrm{PBr}_{3}
-equivariant for the parallel transport actions constructed above. Indeed, the generators
a^{2},b^{2},ab^{2}a^{-1}
of
\mathrm{PBr}_{3}
act by spherical twists on
\mathcal{Q}_{1}
, but – as autoequivalences of the compact category
\operatorname{Tw}\,\mathcal{F}(W_{k})
– two act by spherical twists and one by a product of
k
spherical twists in orthogonal objects for
k>1
. When
k>1
, the representation

\mathrm{PBr}_{3}\to\operatorname{Auteq}(\operatorname{Tw}\,\mathcal{F}(W_{k}))

is not especially natural from the viewpoint of the subcategory
\operatorname{Tw}\,\mathcal{Q}_{k}\subset\operatorname{Tw}\,\mathcal{F}(W_{k})
, since that subcategory does not contain the objects given by the Lens space with non-trivial local systems. The equivalence
\mathcal{Q}_{1}\simeq\mathcal{Q}_{k}
induces a different
\mathrm{PBr}_{3}
action on
\mathcal{Q}_{k}
, in which all three ‘standard’ generators are spherical twists: the Lens space twist is replaced just by
T_{S_{1}}
where
S_{1}
is the spherical object corresponding to the trivial local system.

4.7.
B-side twists

We now revert back to the specific crepant resolution
Y_{k}\to\operatorname{Spec}R_{k}
constructed in Lemma
3.1
, for any
\mathbb{K}
, and any
k\geqslant 0
.

For any
\mathbb{K}
and any
k\geqslant 0
, the threefold
Y_{k}
has spherical objects
\mathcal{S}_{i}=\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{C}_{i}}(-1)
for
i=1,2
corresponding to the two
(-1,-1)
-curves in Lemma
3.1
. Both give rise to spherical twists. As on the A-side, the third generator depends on whether
k=0
or not.

•

When
k=0
, and
\mathrm{char}\,\mathbb{K}=0
, we can consider the twist autoequivalence over the affine line
\mathbb{K}[x]
considered in
[
17
, Example 6.4]
, which we denote
\uptau_{\mathrm{mix}}
.

•

When
k>0
, regardless of the characteristic, since the mutation functors give derived equivalences between the NCCRs it can be seen directly that the mapping cone
\mathcal{S}_{1}\to\mathcal{S}_{2}
on the non-trivial morphism is fat-spherical. We write
\uptau_{\mathrm{fat}}
for its associated twist, which is spherical over
\mathbb{K}[x]/x^{k}
. Hence this third generator is a ‘genuine’ spherical object if and only if
k=1
.

Paralleling the monodromy actions by symplectomorphisms gives the following.

Lemma 4.26
.

With notation as above:

(1)

The category
\mathcal{C}_{0}
admits an action of the mixed braid group
\mathrm{MBr}_{3}
.

(2)

For
k>0
, the category
\mathcal{C}_{k}
admits an action of the pure braid group
\mathrm{PBr}_{3}
.

In both cases, one may take the spherical twists in the objects
\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{C}_{i}}(-1)
to correspond to the elements
a^{2}
and
b^{2}
. When
k=0
the third generator is
\uptau_{\mathrm{mix}}
which corresponds to
aba
, and when
k>0
the third generator is
\uptau_{\mathrm{fat}}
which corresponds to
(aba)^{2}
.

Proof.

Part (1) is a special case of results in
[
15
]
; see also
[
17
, Example 6.4]
. The generators of the mixed braid group action are the spherical twists in the two
(-1,-1)
-curves in the resolution, and the family twist
\uptau_{\mathrm{mix}}
. Since the resolution curves move in a surface, the local geometry is modelled on the product of the resolution of a surface singularity with
\operatorname{Spec}\,\mathbb{C}[x]
, and the family twist is essentially the pullback of the twist from one factor. In terms of the usual braid group generators, these correspond to
\{a^{2},b^{2},aba\}
.

When
k>0
and
\mathrm{char}\,\mathbb{K}=0
this is contained in
[
18
]
; the pure braid group generators can be taken either to be given by the spherical twists in the two resolution curves and the spherical twist in their cone, or the spherical twists in the resolution curves and the autoequivalence associated to their union. These correspond to the braid group elements
\{a^{2},b^{2},ab^{2}a^{-1}\}
and
\{a^{2},b^{2},(aba)^{2}\}
respectively. When
\mathrm{char}\,\mathbb{K}=p
these results still hold, since they only rely on the mutation functors and the tilting order, which still exist.
∎

Proposition 4.27
.

The following statements hold.

(1)

If
\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{C}
, then the equivalence of categories
\mathcal{Q}_{1}\simeq\mathcal{C}_{1}
of Theorem
1.1
entwines the pure braid group actions, whilst the equivalence
\mathcal{Q}_{0}\simeq\mathcal{C}_{0}
entwines the mixed braid group actions on the level of objects.

(2)

If
\mathrm{char}\,\mathbb{K}=p>2
then the equivalence
\mathcal{Q}_{p}\simeq\mathcal{C}_{p}
of Theorem
1.1
entwines the action of the pure braid group actions, on the level of objects.

Proof.

In Lemma
4.15
and
4.11
we showed that the representations
\mathrm{MBr}_{3}\to\uppi_{0}\,\mathrm{Symp}(W_{0})
respectively
\mathrm{PBr}_{3}\to\uppi_{0}\,\mathrm{Symp}(W_{k})
take the generators
a^{2},b^{2}
to the Dehn twists in the core spheres
\uptau_{Q_{1}},\uptau_{Q_{2}}
. The equivalence of Theorem
1.1
take the sphericals
Q_{i}
to the simple modules corresponding to the two vertices of the cyclic quiver. In turn, these go to the sheaves
\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{C}_{i}}(-1)
, hence take the twists
\uptau_{Q_{i}}
to the spherical twists in these sheaves.

For
W_{1}
, when
\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{C}
the third generator is again a spherical twist on both sides (now in the cone), and the result follows. When
\mathrm{char}\,\mathbb{K}=p
, the third generator on both sides is now fat spherical. However, the results of
[
50
]
are sufficient only to infer that the Lens space twist
\uptau_{L}
and the appropriate mapping cone agree object-wise. Hence, we can only conclude that the actions entwine on the level of objects.

For
W_{0}
, the generator
aba
of
\mathrm{MBr}_{3}
is the lift of the Dehn twist in
T^{*}S^{2}
for
W_{0}
and is the ‘family spherical twist’ for
\mathcal{C}_{0}
. In both cases, this is a two-dimensional twist which exchanges the two simples and shifts each of them by
[-1]
, which is sufficient to determine the action on objects.
∎

Remark 4.28
.

One could probably upgrade the statement for
\mathcal{C}_{0},\mathcal{Q}_{0}
to a full entwining of actions by proving mirror symmetry for slightly larger categories which incorporates the non-compact object defining the appropriate twist, cf. Remark
4.12
.

4.8.
Faithfulness

Faithfulness of the pure braid group action for flopping contractions was first established in
[
29
]
, for the case
\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{C}
. When
\mathrm{char}\,\mathbb{K}=p
the faithfulness still holds, since all techniques used only rely on properties of noncommutative resolutions, mutation functors, torsion pairs and the tilting order, which are characteristic independent.

Recall that the group
\mathrm{Symp}(W_{p})
has a central
\mathbb{Z}
-extension of ‘graded’ symplectomorphisms, and there is a corresponding graded symplectic mapping class group
\uppi_{0}\,\mathrm{Symp}_{gr}(W_{p})
which acts by autoequivalences on the compact Fukaya category (the usual mapping class group acts by autoequivalences up to shift).

Corollary 4.29
.

If
p=1
or
p>2
is prime, then the natural representation
\uprho_{p}\colon\mathrm{PBr}_{3}\to\uppi_{0}\,\mathrm{Symp}_{gr}(W_{p})
is faithful.

Proof.

Appealing to Corollary
3.13
,
\mathcal{Q}_{1}\simeq\mathcal{C}_{1}
in characteristic zero, or
\mathcal{Q}_{p}\simeq\mathcal{C}_{p}
in characteristic
p>2
. Either way, by
[
29
]
and the above paragraph, the natural homomorphism

\mathrm{PBr}_{3}\to\operatorname{Auteq}\mathcal{C}_{k}

from Lemma
4.26
is injective. Even although in Proposition
4.27
we don’t know functorially that the pure braid actions entwine under the equivalence
\mathcal{Q}_{p}\simeq\mathcal{C}_{p}
, it is still true that the natural homomorphism

(4.8)

\mathrm{PBr}_{3}\to\operatorname{Auteq}\mathcal{Q}_{p}

is injective. This is since injectivity in
[
29
]
is determined by Deligne normal form and dimensions of Ext groups, and this information is determined entirely by the action of the functors on objects. Now by Lemma
4.15
the injective homomorphism (
4.8
) factors as

\mathrm{PBr}_{3}\to\uppi_{0}\,\mathrm{Symp}_{gr}(W_{k})\to\operatorname{Auteq}\mathcal{Q}_{p},

and so it follows that the first map must also be injective.
∎

Using Remark
4.16
, one can improve this when
k=1
to a faithful representation
\mathrm{PBr}_{3}\to\uppi_{0}\mathrm{Symp}_{ct}(W_{1})
.

5.
The wrapped Fukaya category and Koszul Duality

In this section we lift the equivalence
\mathcal{Q}_{k}\simeq\mathcal{C}_{k}
, over the appropriate coefficient field, to yield a new description and comparison of the wrapped category of
W_{k}
and the relative singularity category of
Y_{k}
. This involves
A_{\infty}
-Koszul duality, which we now briefly recall, following
[
48
]
,
[
35
]
and
[
19
]
.

For an
A_{\infty}
-category
\mathcal{A}
, recall that we have categories of proper and perfect modules

\mathcal{A}^{per}\subset\mathcal{A}^{mod}\supset\mathcal{A}^{prop}.

We say
\mathcal{A}
is homologically smooth if the diagonal bimodule is perfect; in this case,
\mathcal{A}^{prop}\subset\mathcal{A}^{per}
.

5.1.
A-side Koszul duality

Consider a Stein manifold
X
containing distinguished compact Lagrangians
L_{i}
and dual non-compact Lagrangian discs
T_{i}
; we will always consider a plumbing with the
L_{i}
being cores and the
T_{i}
co-cores (cotangent fibres). Note that, in this setting, the
\{T_{i}\}
are known to generate the wrapped Fukaya category
\mathcal{W}(X)
by
[
13
]
. We have compact and wrapped endomorphism algebras
\mathcal{Q}=\oplus_{i,j}CF^{*}(L_{i},L_{j})
and
\mathcal{W}=\oplus_{i,j}CW^{*}(T_{i},T_{j})
, which are
A_{\infty}
-algebras naturally augmented over the semisimple ring
\mathbf{k}=\oplus_{i}\mathbb{K}
generated by the identity idempotents of the objects. It is known that the wrapped Fukaya category of any Stein manifold is homologically smooth, by deep results of Chantraine, Dmitroglou Rizell, Ghiggini and Golovko
[
13
]
.

We impose the following
hypotheses
:
H^{*}(\mathcal{Q})
is concentrated in non-negative degrees,
H^{0}(\mathcal{Q})=\mathbf{k}
, and
H^{*}(\mathcal{W})
is concentrated in non-positive degrees. The first two hold for the double bubble plumbings by Theorem
1.1
, whilst the last holds for the wrapped category of a double bubble by
[
3
]
.

Given that, Ekholm and Lekili prove that there is an equivalence

(5.1)

\mathcal{Q}\simeq\operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal{W}}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k})

and there is a natural map to a certain completion

(5.2)

\mathcal{W}\to\widehat{\mathcal{W}}\simeq\operatorname{RHom}_{\mathcal{Q}}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}).

When no completion is necessary, we say the compact and wrapped categories are Koszul dual; in general, the compact category is dual to
\widehat{\mathcal{W}}
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
be
A_{\infty}
-categories and
F\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
a fully faithful functor. Write
\Gamma(F)
for the graph bimodule of
F
, so

\Gamma(F)(Y,X)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}hom_{\mathcal{B}}(Y,F(X)),\qquad X\in\mathrm{Ob}\,\mathcal{A},\ Y\in\mathrm{Ob}\,\mathcal{B}.

Let
\mathcal{Y}
denote the left Yoneda functor
\mathcal{B}^{op}\to(\mathcal{B}^{op})^{mod}
.
We will make use of the following result of Lekili and Ueda.

Proposition 5.1
.

Suppose that:

(1)

\mathcal{A}
is generated by finitely many spherical objects
\{S_{i}\}
;

(2)

For any
Y,Y^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{B}
the complex
hom_{\mathcal{B}}(Y,Y^{\prime})
is bounded above (resp. below);

(3)

For any
X\in\mathcal{A}
and
Y\in\mathcal{B}
the complex
hom_{\mathcal{B}}(Y,F(X))
of
\mathbb{K}
-modules is perfect;

(4)

There is a quasi-equivalence of functors
T_{F(S_{1})}\circ\cdots\circ T_{F(S_{n})}\simeq[m]
for a non-trivial negative (resp. positive) integer
m
.

Then the functor
\Gamma(F)\otimes_{\mathcal{B}}\mathcal{Y}(-):\mathcal{B}^{op}\to(\mathcal{A}^{op})^{mod}
is fully faithful.

Proof.

This is exactly
[
45
, Proposition 6.5]
. ∎

Proposition 5.2
.

Let
k=1
and
\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{C}
or
k>2
be prime and
\mathrm{char}\,\mathbb{K}=k
. Then
\mathcal{Q}_{k}
is Koszul dual to
\mathcal{W}_{k}
.

Proof.

Note that, by reversing the sign of the symplectic form and exchanging left and right modules, there is an equivalence between the exact Fukaya category and its opposite, see
[
60
, Appendix A]
. By Corollary
4.22
the category
\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{Q}_{k}
is generated by the spherical objects given by the cores, which furthermore split-generate if we work in the right characteristic. The dual collection of cotangent fibres
T_{1}\oplus T_{2}
gives a generating subcategory
\mathcal{B}=\mathcal{W}_{k}\subset\mathcal{W}(W_{k})
, which satisfies the condition that complexes
hom_{\mathcal{B}}
are bounded above as discussed previously. The crucial hypothesis on a product of twists giving a shift is given by Lemma
4.21
.
Applying Proposition
5.1
, we have a fully faithful functor
\mathcal{W}_{k}\to(\mathcal{Q}_{k})^{mod}
, which sends the generator
T_{1}\oplus T_{2}
to
\mathbf{k}
. This implies the result, c.f. the proof of
[
45
, Theorem 6.11]
.
∎

Remark 5.3
.

A sufficient criterion for
\mathcal{Q}
and
\mathcal{W}
to be Koszul dual (no completion required) is that
H^{*}(\mathcal{W})
is concentrated in non-positive degrees and finite-dimensional in each degree; in fact, an argument due to Kalck-Yang
[
35
]
show that it is even sufficient to have
H^{0}(\mathcal{W})
be finite-dimensional. The double-bubble plumbing
W_{k}
can be presented as the result of Morse-Bott surgery on
T^{*}S^{3}
, attaching the cotangent bundle of a solid torus to the Legendrian conormal torus of an unknot
S^{1}\subset S^{3}
. This gives a description of the wrapped Floer complex of the cocores in terms of binormal chords between an unknot and a distinct point (corresponding to the handle that is attached to yield
T^{*}S^{3}
from
T^{*}\mathbb{R}^{3}
). Assuming an extension of the ‘surgery’ relation between Lagrangian and Legendrian invariants from
[
7
,
19
]
from the case of handle attachment to Morse-Bott handle attachment, one can presumably use such a presentation to establish finite-dimensionality of
H^{0}(\mathcal{W})
directly. This would yield the Koszul duality statement without requiring the detour via Lemma
4.21
. In contrast, both
CW^{0}
and
HW^{0}
are infinite-dimensional for the plumbing
W_{0}
.

5.2.
B-side Koszul duality

For any
k\geqslant 1
consider again the flopping contraction
Y_{k}\to\operatorname{Spec}(R_{k})
over a field
\mathbb{K}
. In this subsection we will show that
\mathcal{C}_{k}
is Koszul dual to the relative singularity
\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\operatorname{coh}Y_{k})/\langle\mathcal{O}_{Y_{k}}\rangle
, following
[
35
]
. An advantage of the B-side is that this Koszul duality works over all
k\geqslant 1
and all
\mathbb{K}
.

Since we are working algebraically (instead of complete locally as in
[
35
]
), we must first resolve the slightly subtle issue of whether our categories are idempotent complete. This is taken care of in the following two results.

Lemma 5.4
.

Suppose that
R
is a 3-sCY excellent normal domain with a unique singular point, which admits an NCCR
\mathrm{End}_{R}(M)
where
M
decomposes into rank one
R
-modules. Then
\underline{\mathrm{CM}}\,R\to\underline{\mathrm{CM}}\,\widehat{R}
is an equivalence, and in particular,
\underline{\mathrm{CM}}\,R
is idempotent complete.

Proof.

Since the assumptions imply that
R
is an isolated G-ring, it is known generally
[
38
, A.1]
that the completion functor
F\colon\underline{\mathrm{CM}}\,R\to\underline{\mathrm{CM}}\,\widehat{R}
is an equivalence up to summands, so we just need to prove that
F
is essentially surjective. Consider an arbitrary
X\in\underline{\mathrm{CM}}\,\widehat{R}
. Since NCCRs pass to the completion
F{M}
is a cluster tilting object
[
31
, 5.5]
, so by
[
31
, 4.12]
there exists a triangle

Y_{0}\xrightarrow{h}Y_{1}\to X\to

with
Y_{i}\in\mathrm{add}\,F{M}
. By assumption
M
decomposes into rank one modules
M\cong\bigoplus L_{i}
say, so
FM\cong\bigoplus FL_{i}
. Since each
FL_{i}
has rank one, each is still indecomposable. Hence by Krull–Schimdt both
Y_{i}
are direct sums of the form
\bigoplus(FL_{i})^{\oplus a_{i}}
, and thus are in the image of
F
. Say
Y_{i}=FM_{i}
. We already know that
F
is fully faithful, so
h=Fg
for some
g\colon M_{0}\to M_{1}
. Set
Y=\mathrm{Cone}\,g
, then it follows
FY\cong X
, since both are the cone on
h=Fg
.
∎

Corollary 5.5
.

For all
k\geqslant 1
, and any
\mathbb{K}
, the singularity category
\underline{\mathrm{CM}}\,R_{k}
and the relative singularity category
\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\operatorname{coh}Y_{k})/\langle\mathcal{O}_{Y_{k}}\rangle
are both idempotent complete.

Proof.

Since
R_{k}
admits an NCCR by Proposition
3.3
which is clearly a direct sum of rank one
R_{k}
-modules, using Lemma
5.4
we see that
\underline{\mathrm{CM}}\,R_{k}
is idempotent complete. The fact that the relative singularity is idempotent complete follows immediately from this using Schlichting’s negative K-Theory (see
[
12
, Theorem 3.2]
).
∎

It then follows that the category
\mathcal{C}_{k}
and the relative singularity category are Koszul dual.

Proposition 5.6
.

For any
k\geqslant 1
and any
\mathbb{K}
,
\mathcal{C}_{k}\simeq\operatorname{per}(A)
and
\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\operatorname{coh}Y_{k})/\langle\mathcal{O}_{Y_{k}}\rangle\simeq\operatorname{per}(A^{!})
, with
A^{!!}=A
up to quasi-isomorphism.

Proof.

By
[
35
, Corollary 2.12(a)]
, there is a DG-algebra
B
such that
\operatorname{per}(B)
is equivalent to the idempotent completion of the relative singularity category. Hence, using Corollary
5.5
,
\operatorname{per}(B)\simeq\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\operatorname{coh}Y_{k})/\langle\mathcal{O}_{Y_{k}}\rangle
itself.

Consider the
A_{\infty}
-algebra
A=\mathbf{R}\mathrm{End}_{\Lambda}(\mathcal{S})
. We already know that
\mathcal{C}_{k}\simeq\operatorname{per}(A)
, and further that
A^{!!}=A
(see e.g.
[
35
, 2.7]
), so it suffices to show that
A^{!}=B
. It is easy to check that
B^{!}=A
up to quasi-isomorphism (see e.g.
[
35
, 2.6]
), thus
B^{!!}=A^{!}
. Hence it remains to justify why
B=B^{!!}
, which is much harder.

As in the A-side (Remark
5.3
), the difficultly is in proving that the non-positive DGA
B
is finite dimensional in each degree; given this, the fact
B^{!!}=B
is standard
[
35
, Theorem 2.8(b)]
. The key point here is that we need the auxiliary data in the form of the existence of the NCCR
\Lambda
, which allows us to say that all
\Lambda/\Lambda e\Lambda
-modules have finite projective dimension as a
\Lambda
-module. We can then appeal directly to
[
35
, Corollary 2.13(i)]
to deduce that
B
is finite dimensional in each degree, with the two main points being that
H^{0}(B)
is the contraction algebra, and thus is finite dimensional since
k\geqslant 1
, and
\mathrm{D}_{fd}(B)\subseteq\operatorname{per}(B)
due to the existence of the NCCR.
∎

5.3.
Matching the A- and B-sides

The previous subsections §
5.1
and §
5.2
combine to give the following, which lifts Theorem
1.1
to include non-compact objects.

Corollary 5.7
.

For
k=1
and
\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{C}
or
k>2
prime and
\mathbb{K}
of characteristic
k
, there is an equivalence of categories
\mathcal{W}(W_{k};\mathbb{K})\simeq\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\operatorname{coh}Y_{k})/\langle\mathcal{O}_{Y_{k}}\rangle
.

Proof.

Corollary
3.13
is proved by establishing that
\mathcal{Q}_{k}\simeq\operatorname{per}(A)\simeq\mathcal{C}_{k}
. Hence combining Propositions
5.2
and
5.6
it follows that
\mathcal{W}(W_{k};\mathbb{K})\simeq\operatorname{per}(A^{!})\simeq\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\operatorname{coh}Y_{k})/\langle\mathcal{O}_{Y_{k}}\rangle
.
∎

Corollary 5.8
.

Suppose
k=1
and
\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{C}
or
k>2
is prime and
\mathbb{K}
has characteristic
k
. The wrapped Floer cohomology algebra
HW^{*}(T_{q_{0}}^{*}\oplus T_{q_{1}}^{*},T_{q_{0}}^{*}\oplus T_{q_{1}}^{*};\mathbb{K})
of the cocores to the core components is the Ginzburg
dg
-algebra of the potential
(ef)^{k+1}
on the two-cycle quiver.

We remind the reader of our standing abuse of notation in the finite characteristic case, where the Ginzburg algebra is not strictly well-defined given issues with cyclic permutation and differentiation. But the coherent interpretation of the statement is correct, in particular,
HW^{0}
is the corresponding Jacobian algebra, i.e. the quotient of the path algebra by the ideal killing paths of length
2k+1
.

6.
Classification of Spherical Objects

In this section, we consider the 3-fold flopping contraction
f\colon Y_{k}\to\operatorname{Spec}R_{k}
, with
k\geqslant 1
, over any
\mathbb{K}
, and we classify all fat-spherical objects in the category
\mathcal{C}_{k}
. Our main result is that there are only three, up to shift and up to the action of the pure braid group.

To ease notation, throughout this section we fix some
k\geqslant 1
and henceforth drop all mention of it from the notation. The flopping contraction

\mathrm{C}_{1}

. Since

is a flopping contraction, we have

\mathcal{C}=\{a\in\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\operatorname{coh}Y)\mid\mathbf{R}f_{*}a=0\},

and across the fixed equivalence (
6.1
),
\mathcal{C}
is equivalent to the subcategory of
\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\operatorname{mod}\Lambda)
consisting of those complexes whose cohomology groups are all annihilated by
e
, or in other words, those complexes whose cohomology groups are
\Lambda_{\operatorname{con}}
-modules.

Remark 6.1
.

There are various t-structures on
\mathcal{C}
. However, throughout this section, for
a\in\mathcal{C}
we will always write
\mathrm{H}^{*}(-)
for cohomology with respect to the standard t-structure in
\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\operatorname{mod}\Lambda)
. Equivalently, we could always work in
\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\operatorname{coh}Y)
, and take cohomology with respect to the perverse t-structure (with perversity
p=-1
). Further, for
a\in\operatorname{mod}\Lambda_{\operatorname{con}}
, we will often write
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(a,a)
for
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(\Psi^{-1}a,\Psi^{-1}a)
, which is the same as
\mathrm{Hom}_{\Lambda}(a,a)
.

A key feature of below is that whilst the normal bundle of a curve being flopped does not change, the normal bundle of other curves it intersects with can change. Algebraically, this corresponds to the fact that the quiver mutation of (
6.2
) changes the algebra (and introduces a loop) if and only if
k>1
. Thus, below the complexity of our argument increases slightly in the
k>1
case, although the main ideas remain the same.

6.1.
Mutation Functors

We recall next the
mutation functors

\Phi_{1}
and
\Phi_{2}
corresponding to mutation between the NCCRs of
R
at vertex
1
, and vertex
2
respectively. These form a representation of the Deligne groupoid, as follows:

\scriptstyle\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\Lambda)
\scriptstyle\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\Lambda_{1})
\scriptstyle\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\Lambda_{12})
\scriptstyle\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\Lambda_{121})
\scriptstyle\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\Lambda_{21})
\scriptstyle\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\Lambda_{2})
\scriptstyle\Phi_{1}
\scriptstyle\Phi_{1}
\scriptstyle\Phi_{2}
\scriptstyle\Phi_{2}
\scriptstyle\Phi_{1}
\scriptstyle\Phi_{1}
\scriptstyle\Phi_{2}
\scriptstyle\Phi_{2}
\scriptstyle\Phi_{1}
\scriptstyle\Phi_{1}
\scriptstyle\Phi_{2}
\scriptstyle\Phi_{2}

where the algebras
\Lambda,\Lambda_{1},\Lambda_{2},\Lambda_{12},\Lambda_{21},\Lambda_{121}
are the six NCCRs corresponding to the six crepant resolutions of
\operatorname{Spec}R
, and
\Lambda
is the NCCR in Lemma
3.5
. It is possible to present the other NCCRs as quivers with relations, but we refrain from doing this here.

As explained in
[
29
, Remark 4.7]
, using only the tilting order, there is a functorial isomorphism
\Phi_{1}\Phi_{2}\Phi_{1}\cong\Phi_{2}\Phi_{1}\Phi_{2}
. By slight abuse of notation, we write
\mathcal{S}_{1},\mathcal{S}_{2}
for the simple modules for the NCCRs, regardless of which NCCR is under consideration. The labelling is consistent, so that mutation
\Phi_{i}
always shifts
\mathcal{S}_{i}
.

Algebraically, the mutation functors can always be described as
\mathbf{R}\mathrm{Hom}(T_{i},-)
where
T_{i}
is a certain tilting module of projective dimension one. From our perspective, the known facts that we require are contained in the following two lemmas.

Lemma 6.2
.

Let
x
be a finite length module viewed as a complex in homological degree zero. Then for
i\in\{1,2\}
, the following statements hold.

(1)

\mathrm{H}^{j}(\Phi_{i}(x))=0
unless
j=0,1
.

(2)

\mathrm{H}^{j}(\Phi_{i}^{-1}(x))=0
unless
j=-1,0
.

(3)

If
\mathrm{Hom}(x,\mathcal{S}_{i})=0
then
\mathrm{H}^{j}(\Phi_{i}(x))=0
for all
j\neq 0
.

(4)

If
\mathrm{Hom}(\mathcal{S}_{i},x)=0
then
\mathrm{H}^{j}(\Phi_{i}^{-1}(x))=0
for all
j\neq 0
.

Proof.

(1) & (2) are a direct consequence of the fact that
T_{i}
is a tilting module, and so has projective dimension one.

(3) & (4) are
[
68
, Corollary 5.10]
, which needs
x
to be finite length.
∎

As notation, set
M_{1}=\mathrm{Cone}(\mathcal{S}_{1}[-1]\to\mathcal{S}_{2})
, and
M_{2}=\mathrm{Cone}(\mathcal{S}_{2}[-1]\to\mathcal{S}_{1})
.

Lemma 6.3
.

The following statements hold.

(1)

\Phi_{1}(\mathcal{S}_{1})=\mathcal{S}_{1}[-1]
,
\Phi_{1}(\mathcal{S}_{2})=M_{1}
and
\Phi_{1}(M_{2})=\mathcal{S}_{2}
.

(2)

\Phi_{2}(\mathcal{S}_{2})=\mathcal{S}_{2}[-1]
,
\Phi_{2}(\mathcal{S}_{1})=M_{2}
and
\Phi_{2}(M_{1})=\mathcal{S}_{1}
.

(3)

The composition
\Phi_{1}\Phi_{2}\Phi_{1}
sends
\mathcal{S}_{1}\mapsto\mathcal{S}_{2}[-1]
,
\mathcal{S}_{2}\mapsto\mathcal{S}_{1}[-1]
, and further if
a\in\operatorname{mod}\Lambda_{\operatorname{con}}
, then
a\mapsto x[-1]
for some
x\in\operatorname{mod}\Lambda_{\operatorname{con}}
.

Proof.

(1) The fact that
\Phi_{i}(\mathcal{S}_{i})=\mathcal{S}_{i}[-1]
is
[
68
, 4.15]
. The fact that
\Phi_{1}(\mathcal{S}_{2})=M_{1}
follows using the same method: by torsion pairs
\Phi_{1}(\mathcal{S}_{2})
is a module in degree zero, and the dimension vector of this module can be determined using the exchange sequences, which are
[
33
, 5.29]
. The final statement
\Phi_{1}(M_{2})=\mathcal{S}_{2}
follows from the first two facts, and applying
\Phi_{1}
to the exact sequence
0\to\mathcal{S}_{1}\to M_{2}\to\mathcal{S}_{2}\to 0
. All of Part (2) follows by symmetry.
For (3), the statement that
\mathcal{S}_{1}\mapsto\mathcal{S}_{2}[-1]
follows from
[
18
, (3.I)]
, which shows that
\Phi_{1}\Phi_{2}\Phi_{1}
is isomorphic to a direct mutation functor, together with
[
68
, 4.15]
which shows simples shift under mutation. The fact that
\mathcal{S}_{1}
gets sent to
\mathcal{S}_{2}[-1]
, as opposed to
\mathcal{S}_{1}[-1]
, is due to our global numbering conventions here, and is explained by the fact
(\upvartheta_{1},\upvartheta_{2})\mapsto(-\upvartheta_{2},-\upvartheta_{1})
underneath
[
18
, (3.I)]
. The other statement
\mathcal{S}_{2}\mapsto\mathcal{S}_{1}[-1]
follows by symmetry. The final statement follows, since every module is filtered by simples.
∎

Remark 6.4
.

For
i=1,2
the composition
\Phi_{i}\circ\Phi_{i}
is functorially isomorphic to the spherical twist
T_{\mathcal{S}_{i}}
around the spherical object
\mathcal{S}_{i}

[
18
]
. Thus Lemma
6.3
shows that
T_{\mathcal{S}_{1}}(M_{2})=M_{1}
and
T_{\mathcal{S}_{2}}(M_{1})=M_{2}
, which is the B-side analogue of (
4.7
).

6.2.
Representation Theory of Contraction Algebras

Our proof of the classification of fat-spherical objects will track through the functors
\Phi_{i}
in the groupoid above. As such, at a technical level the categories change mildly, although of course all are equivalent.

The six crepant resolutions of
\operatorname{Spec}R
give rise to six versions of the category
\mathcal{C}
, all of which are equivalent. To avoid a proliferation of notation, we will mildly abuse notation, and refer to each simply as
\mathcal{C}
. Further, each crepant resolution has a tilting bundle giving an equivalence to the corresponding NCCR, and again we will abuse notation and write
\Psi
for this equivalence, regardless of which crepant resolution we are considering.

Each of the categories
\mathcal{C}
, across the relevant
\Psi
, is equivalent to the subcategory of the derived category of the NCCR whose cohomology is a module for the corresponding contraction algebra. Since the mutation functors restrict to an equivalence on these subcategories, we summarise this information in the following diagram. The right hand side shows the quiver of the corresponding contraction algebra, where the loops exist if and only if
k>1
.
