We write
\Lambda_{\operatorname{con}}
for the first, and
\Upgamma_{\operatorname{con}}
for the second. Note that both depend on
k
, and they are isomorphic if and only if
k=1
. Further,
\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Lambda_{\operatorname{con}}=2+4k
and
\dim_{\mathbb{K}}\Upgamma_{\operatorname{con}}=k+5
.

Remark 6.5
.

The difference between
k=1
and
k>1
is also manifest symplectically. The Stein manifold
W_{k}
has a Lagrangian skeleton
Q_{0}\cup Q_{1}
, but also a Lagrangian skeleton given by the union of one
Q_{i}
and the Morse-Bott surgery
K
; cf. Example
4.2
, where
K
fibres over a path in the base of the Morse-Bott-Lefschetz fibration of Figure
1
between the outermost two critical points. When
k\neq 1
and this is a Lens space, the endomorphism algebra of the second core (and its wrapped counterpart) differs from that of the first, even though they are derived equivalent.

For our purposes, we only require the following two facts, which follow from an analysis of the representation theory. These will turn out to be the key to understanding how to iteratively apply mutation functors later to ‘improve’ fat spherical objects.

Proposition 6.6
.

Suppose that
a,b\in\operatorname{mod}\Lambda_{\operatorname{con}}
satisfies
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(a,b)=0
. Then either
a
or
b
is filtered by a unique simple. The same result holds for
\Upgamma_{\operatorname{con}}
.

Proof.

We give the proof for
k=1
here. Indeed, when
k=1
there are only six indecomposable
\Lambda_{\operatorname{con}}
-modules, namely the two projective
\Lambda_{\operatorname{con}}
-modules, say
\mathcal{Q}_{1}
and
\mathcal{Q}_{2}
, and the modules
\mathcal{S}_{1}
,
\mathcal{S}_{2}
,
M_{1}
and
M_{2}
. Either by directly computing homomorphism spaces between these very small dimensional quiver representations, or by knitting on the Auslander–Reiten quiver (as proved in §
6.5
), or by computer algebra (e.g. QPA
[
27
,
25
]
), the dimension of the
\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)
with
X
a member of the rows, and
Y
a member of the columns, is summarised in the following table

(6.3)

\begin{array}[]{ccccccc}&\mathcal{Q}_{1}&\mathcal{Q}_{2}&M_{1}&M_{2}&\mathcal{S}_{1}&\mathcal{S}_{2}\\
\mathcal{Q}_{1}&2&1&1&1&1&0\\
\mathcal{Q}_{2}&1&2&1&1&0&1\\
M_{1}&1&1&1&1&1&0\\
M_{2}&1&1&1&1&0&1\\
\mathcal{S}_{1}&1&0&0&1&1&0\\
\mathcal{S}_{2}&0&1&1&0&0&1\end{array}

Now, if
\mathcal{Q}_{1}
is a summand of
a
, since by assumption
\mathrm{Hom}(a,b)=0
, the only possibility for
b
is
\mathcal{S}_{2}^{\oplus t}
, regardless of what other summands
a
has. Ditto
M_{1}
. Similarly, if
\mathcal{Q}_{2}
is a summand of
a
, then
b
is
\mathcal{S}_{1}^{\oplus t}
. Ditto
M_{2}
. The only remaining options for
a
are the remaining rows and combinations of them, so either
\mathcal{S}_{1}^{\oplus s}
,
\mathcal{S}_{1}^{\oplus t}
, or
\mathcal{S}_{1}^{\oplus s}\oplus\mathcal{S}_{2}^{\oplus t}
. In the latter case, if a module is orthogonal to both simples, it is zero. Hence the last two cases are
a
is either
\mathcal{S}_{1}^{\oplus s}
or
\mathcal{S}_{2}^{\oplus t}
.

The general
k>1
proof is similar, but the number of indecomposable modules increases. Since these method of proof uses knitting on the AR quiver (which gives an independent check on the computer algebra claim above), and is quite different to the rest of this section, we delay the full proof until Section
6.5
.
∎

The following is rather similar.

Lemma 6.7
.

There are only four modules
X\in\operatorname{mod}\Lambda_{\operatorname{con}}
for which
\mathrm{End}_{\mathcal{C}}(X)=\mathbb{K}
. They are:
\mathcal{S}_{1}
,
\mathcal{S}_{2}
,
M_{1}
and
M_{2}
. The same statement holds for
X\in\operatorname{mod}\Upgamma_{\operatorname{con}}
.

Proof.

For the case
k=1
, this follows directly from observing the diagonal entries in the table (
6.3
). The
k>1
case again is similar, and uses knitting, and consequently we again delay the proof until Section
6.5
.
∎

6.3.
Induction on Length

With the mild abuse of notation as outlined in Section
6.2
, for
a\in\mathcal{C}
, write
t
for the maximum
j
such that
\mathrm{H}^{j}(\Psi a)\neq 0
, and
b
for the minimum
j
such that
\mathrm{H}^{j}(\Psi a)\neq 0
. The
homological length
of
a\in\mathcal{C}
is defined to be
\ell(a)=t-b
. In particular,
\ell(a)=0
if and only if
\Psi a
is in a single homological degree, which holds if and only if
\Psi a
is a shift of a
\Lambda_{\operatorname{con}}
-module (or
\Upgamma_{\operatorname{con}}
-module, depending which
\mathcal{C}
we are considering).

Remark 6.8
.

The homological length used here is very different to the length invariant used to induct in the surfaces case
[
30
]
. Indeed, comparing to Remark
6.1
, in the two-dimensional case there are again two natural 2-CY categories: the derived category of modules over the preprojective algebra, and the derived category of the resolution (the analogues in our setting are respectively
\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\operatorname{mod}\Lambda)
and
\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\operatorname{coh}Y)
).
Op. cit
. works with the latter rather than the former, which leads to a more complicated induction.

Lemma 6.9
.

Suppose that
a\in\mathcal{C}
satisfies
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(a,a[i])=0
for all
i<0
. If
\ell(a)>0
, then
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathrm{H}^{t}(\Psi a),\mathrm{H}^{b}(\Psi a))=0
.

Proof.

This follows from the spectral sequence

E_{2}^{p,q}=\bigoplus_{i}\mathrm{Hom}^{p}(\mathrm{H}^{i}(\Psi a),\mathrm{H}^{i+q}(\Psi a))\Rightarrow\mathrm{Hom}^{p+q}(\Psi a,\Psi a).

The bottom left of the spectral sequence is
E_{2}^{0,-\ell(a)}=\mathrm{Hom}(\mathrm{H}^{t}(\Psi a),\mathrm{H}^{b}(\Psi a))
, and so this survives to
E_{\infty}
, to give part of
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits}(\Psi a,\Psi a[-\ell(a)])
. Since by assumption
\Psi a
has no negative Exts, and
\ell(a)>0
, it follows that
E_{2}^{0,-\ell(a)}=0
, proving the assertion.
∎

The following very simple spectral sequence argument is one of our key technical lemmas. It demonstrates why we don’t study the twist functors directly in dimension three: in contrast, the spectral sequence for the twists does not degenerate immediately, since it has
E_{2}^{0,q}
,
E_{2}^{1,q}
, and
E_{2}^{2,q}
. Thus, our strategy is to use the mutation functors to simplify first (as for surfaces), then afterwards put everything in terms of the twists.

Lemma 6.10
.

If
a\in\mathcal{C}
with
\ell(a)>0
, write
\mathrm{H}^{t}=\mathrm{H}^{t}(\Psi a)
for the top cohomology, and
\mathrm{H}^{b}=\mathrm{H}^{b}(\Psi a)
for the bottom. Then for
i\in\{0,1\}
, the following statements hold.

(1)

If
\mathrm{H}^{1}\bigl(\Phi_{i}(\mathrm{H}^{t})\bigr)=0
and
\mathrm{H}^{0}\bigl(\Phi_{i}(\mathrm{H}^{b})\bigr)=0
, then
\ell(\Phi_{i}(a))<\ell(a)
.

(2)

If
\mathrm{H}^{0}\bigl(\Phi_{i}^{-1}(\mathrm{H}^{t})\bigr)=0
and
\mathrm{H}^{-1}\bigl(\Phi_{i}^{-1}(\mathrm{H}^{b})\bigr)=0
, then
\ell(\Phi_{i}^{-1}(a))<\ell(a)
.

Proof.

(1) Consider the spectral sequence

E_{2}^{p,q}=\mathrm{H}^{p}\bigl(\Phi_{i}(\mathrm{H}^{q}(\Psi a))\bigr)\Rightarrow\mathrm{H}^{p+q}\bigl(\Phi_{i}(\Psi a)\bigr)

By Lemma
6.2
(
1
), only
E_{2}^{0,q}
and
E_{2}^{1,q}
can possibly be non-zero, so the spectral sequence degenerates immediately. The bottom left entry is
\mathrm{H}^{0}(\Phi_{i}(\mathrm{H}^{b}))
and the top right entry is
\mathrm{H}^{1}(\Phi_{i}(\mathrm{H}^{t}))
. If these are both zero, it follows that in the resulting complex
\Phi_{i}(\Psi a)
, the bottom cohomology is in homological degree
b+1
, and the top cohomology is in homological degree
t
. Hence the complex has become smaller, and
\ell(\Phi_{i}(\Psi a))<\ell(a)
.

(2) This is very similar, using

E_{2}^{p,q}=\mathrm{H}^{p}\bigl(\Phi^{-1}_{i}(\mathrm{H}^{q}(\Psi a))\bigr)\Rightarrow\mathrm{H}^{p+q}\bigl(\Phi^{-1}_{i}(\Psi a)\bigr).

Now by Lemma
6.2
(
2
) the only non-zero terms are
E_{2}^{-1,q}
and
E_{2}^{0,q}
; the spectral sequence still degenerates immediately.
∎

The following is the main technical result of this section, and gives a constructive way of simplifying the complex
a
by applying mutation functors.

Theorem 6.11
.

Suppose that
a\in\mathcal{C}
satisfies
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(a,a[i])=0
for all
i<0
, and
\ell(a)>0
.

(1)

Either
\mathrm{H}^{t}(\Psi a)
or
\mathrm{H}^{b}(\Psi a)
is filtered by a unique simple module
\mathcal{S}_{i}
, with
i\in\{0,1\}
.

(2)

When
\mathrm{H}^{b}(\Psi a)
is filtered only by
\mathcal{S}_{i}
, applying
\Phi_{i}
decreases the length
\ell
.

(3)

When
\mathrm{H}^{t}(\Psi a)
is filtered only by
\mathcal{S}_{i}
, applying
\Phi_{i}^{-1}
decreases the length
\ell
.

Proof.

(1) By Lemma
6.9
,
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathrm{H}^{t},\mathrm{H}^{b})=0
, so the result follows from the key representation theory fact in Proposition
6.6
.

(2) Since
\Phi_{i}(\mathcal{S}_{i})=\mathcal{S}_{i}[-1]
by Lemma
6.3
, by induction on the length of the filtration of
\mathrm{H}^{b}
, it follows that
\mathrm{H}^{0}(\Phi_{i}(\mathrm{H}^{b}))=0
. Further,
\mathrm{Hom}(\mathrm{H}^{t},\mathrm{H}^{b})=0
implies
\mathrm{Hom}(\mathrm{H}^{t},\mathcal{S}_{i})=0
, so by Lemma
6.2
(
3
)
\mathrm{H}^{1}(\Phi_{i}(\mathrm{H}^{t}))=0
. Combining, using Lemma
6.10
(
1
) we see that
\ell(\Phi_{i}(a))<\ell(a)
.

(3) This is very similar, using
\Phi_{i}^{-1}(\mathcal{S}_{i})=\mathcal{S}_{i}[1]
, and Lemmas
6.2
(
4
) and
6.10
(
2
).
∎

For any element
\upbeta
of the Deligne groupoid of the hyperplane arrangement mentioned at the start of Section
6.1
, cf. the diagram at the start of that section, there is a composition of mutation functors giving an equivalence
\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\Lambda)\to\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\Lambda_{\upbeta})
from the NCCR at the base vertex to that labelling the chamber associated to
\upbeta
. Recall also that in the notational convention from Section
6.2
, we identify
\mathcal{C}
with a subcategory of any
\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\Lambda)
and hence the mutation functors act on elements of
\mathcal{C}
.

Corollary 6.12
.

Suppose that
a\in\mathcal{C}
satisfies
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(a,a[i])=0
for all
i<0
. Then there exists a composition of mutation functors
F\colon\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\Lambda)\to\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\Lambda_{\upbeta})
such that
Fa\cong a^{\prime}
, where
a^{\prime}
is a module for the contraction algebra of
\Lambda_{\upbeta}
.

Proof.

By inducting along Theorem
6.11
, it is easy to see that there exists a composition on mutation functors
G
such that
\ell(Ga)=0
. Hence
G(\Psi a)\cong a^{\prime}[j]
where
a^{\prime}
is a module in degree zero, and
j\in\mathbb{Z}
. Since
\Psi a\in\mathcal{C}
, and the mutation functors preserve
\mathcal{C}
, necessarily
a^{\prime}
is a module for the relevant contraction algebra.

Now by Lemma
6.3
(
3
)
\Phi_{1}\Phi_{2}\Phi_{1}\cong\Phi_{2}\Phi_{1}\Phi_{2}
sends every contraction algebra module to a shift of some contraction algebra module. Hence, applying
\Phi_{1}\Phi_{2}\Phi_{1}
or its inverse repeatedly if necessary, we can move
G(\Psi a)
to homological degree zero.
∎

The following is the main result of this subsection.

Corollary 6.13
.

Suppose that
a\in\mathcal{C}
satisfies
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(a,a[i])=0
for all
i<0
, and further
\dim_{k}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(a,a)=1
. Then the following statements hold.

(1)

There exists a composition of mutation functors
F\colon\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\Lambda)\to\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\Lambda_{\upbeta})
such that
Fa
is either
\mathcal{S}_{1}
or
\mathcal{S}_{2}
.

(2)

The complex
a
is fat-spherical, and up to the action of the pure braid group, is either
\mathcal{S}_{1},\mathcal{S}_{2},M_{1}
, or their shifts by
[1]
.

Proof.

(1) By Corollary
6.12
, we can find a composition of mutation functors
F\colon\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\Lambda)\to\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\Lambda_{\upbeta})
such that
Fa\cong a^{\prime}
, where
a^{\prime}
is a
(\Lambda_{\upbeta})_{\operatorname{con}}
-module in homological degree zero. But

\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(a^{\prime},a^{\prime})\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(a,a)=\mathbb{K},

so Lemma
6.7
forces
a^{\prime}
to be either
M_{1}
,
M_{2}
,
\mathcal{S}_{1}
or
\mathcal{S}_{2}
. Since
\Phi_{2}(M_{1})\cong\mathcal{S}_{1}
and
\Phi_{1}(M_{2})\cong\mathcal{S}_{2}
by Lemma
6.3
, in all cases overall we can find a composition of mutation functors taking
a
to either
\mathcal{S}_{1}
or
\mathcal{S}_{2}
.

(2) By (1) there exists
F
such that
Fa
is either
\mathcal{S}_{1}
and
\mathcal{S}_{2}
. Depending on the NCCR
\Lambda_{\upbeta}
, the
\mathcal{S}_{i}
can be either spherical or fat-spherical (when
k=1
they are always spherical). Since autoequivalences preserve both,
a
itself must also be spherical, or fat-spherical. For the last statement, consider the shortest positive chain of mutation functors
\Phi_{\upalpha}\colon\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\Lambda)\to\mathop{\rm{D}^{b}}\nolimits(\Lambda_{\upbeta})
. Since
Fa
is a simple, by torsion pairs
[
29
, (5.B)]

\Phi_{\upalpha}^{-1}Fa
is either a module, or a shift
[1]
of a module. Since
\mathrm{End}_{\mathcal{C}}(\Phi_{\upalpha}^{-1}Fa)
is one-dimensional, by Lemma
6.7
it is either
M_{1}
,
M_{2}
,
\mathcal{S}_{1}
or
\mathcal{S}_{2}
, or their shift
[1]
. Given
\Phi_{1}\Phi_{1}(M_{2})=M_{1}
by Remark
6.4
, the result follows.
∎

6.4.
Symplectic applications

We collect a number of symplectic applications of Corollary
6.13
, which in particular establish several claims from the Introduction. Recall that our basic equivalence
\mathcal{Q}_{p}\simeq\mathcal{C}_{p}
concerns
\mathbb{Z}
-graded categories, and an exact Lagrangian
L\subset W_{p}
(more generally, an exact Lagrangian equipped with a local system) defines an object of the
\mathbb{Z}
-graded Fukaya category precisely when it has vanishing Maslov class. The basic translation of the Corollary is as follows, where by a trivial local system we mean no local system.

Corollary 6.14
.

Let
p=1
or
p>2
be prime. Let
L\subset W_{p}
be a closed connected exact Lagrangian submanifold with vanishing Maslov class, equipped with a rank one
\mathbb{K}
-local system. Then
L
is quasi-isomorphic to a pure braid image of one of the two core components or the Morse-Bott surgery of the core components.

Proof.

By exactness, for any rank one local system
\xi\to L
, the endomorphisms of the corresponding Lagrangian brane reproduce those of the trivial local system, which are in turn given by ordinary cohomology,
HF^{*}(\xi,\xi)\cong HF^{*}(L,L)\cong H^{*}(L;\mathbb{K})
. The hypotheses imply that
HF^{<0}(L,L)=0
and
HF^{0}(L,L)\cong\mathbb{K}
. Under the mirror equivalence
\mathcal{F}(W_{p};\mathbb{K})=D^{\pi}\mathcal{Q}_{p}\simeq\mathcal{C}_{p}
, valid over a field of the appropriate characteristic,
L
(or more generally
\xi\to L
) defines an object
\mathcal{E}_{L}\in\mathcal{C}_{p}
satisfying the hypotheses of Corollary
6.13
. The second statement of the Corollary shows that
\mathcal{E}_{L}
is a pure braid image of one of the simples
\mathcal{S}_{1},\mathcal{S}_{2}
or the module
M_{1}
obtained as the mapping cone. The equivalence
\mathcal{Q}_{p}\simeq\mathcal{C}_{p}
identifies the cores
Q_{i}
with the simples
\mathcal{S}_{i}
, so the result follows. ∎

It follows that every two graded exact Lagrangians in
W_{p}
, with
p=1
or
p>2
prime, have non-empty intersection, which is already not obvious.

Remark 6.15
.

We established in Proposition
2.9
that, in characteristic zero, there is an equivalence
\mathcal{Q}_{p}\simeq\mathcal{Q}_{1}
for any
p>0
. Nonetheless, one cannot obtain restrictions on Lagrangian submanifolds of
W_{p}
from this, because for
p>1
the subcategory
\mathcal{Q}_{p}\subset\mathcal{F}(W_{p};\mathbb{K})
is not split-generating if
\mathrm{char}(\mathbb{K})=0
, and not invariant under the action of the pure braid group, cf. the discussion after Lemma
4.19
and Remark
4.23
. The symplectic applications for Lagrangians in
W_{p}
with
p\neq 1
rely essentially on the equivalence of categories in finite characteristic.

Note that in the case
p>2
, the endomorphisms of the core components and of their surgery themselves differ: the surgery is fat spherical but not spherical.

Corollary 6.16
.

If
p>2
is prime, then every Lagrangian sphere in
W_{p}
admits an orientation such that, after applying a twist by the action of the pure braid group, it becomes quasi-isomorphic to one of the two oriented core components. If
p=1
, the same is true, except that it may also be quasi-isomorphic to a surgery of the two cores.

Identify
H_{3}(W_{p};\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}
with generators the core components
Q_{i}
, with either choice of orientation. The following is the homological analogue for
W_{p}
of the ‘nearby Lagrangian conjecture’, which implies that an exact Lagrangian in the cotangent bundle is homologous to the zero-section. (Note, however, that we require a hypothesis on the Maslov class.).

Corollary 6.17
.

Let
p=1
or
p>2
be prime. If
L\subset W_{p}
is a closed exact Lagrangian submanifold with vanishing Maslov class, then
\pm[L]\in\{(1,0),(0,1),(1,\pm 1)\}\subset\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}
.

Proof.

Take an exact
L\subset W_{p}
with
p>2
; the case
p=1
is analogous. The pure braid group
\mathrm{PBr}_{3}
acts on
W_{p}
by symplectomorphisms, and the induced action on integral homology is trivial. Fix a field
\mathbb{K}
of characteristic
p
. According to Corollary
6.13
, we have
\phi\in\mathrm{PBr}_{3}
for which
\phi(L)
is quasi-isomorphic to a core component, which without loss of generality we take to be
S_{1}
, in
\mathcal{F}(W_{p};\mathbb{K})
. From quasi-isomorphism over
\mathbb{K}
we can draw two conclusions:

(1)

\phi(L)
, and hence
L
, has homology class equal to
[S_{1}]\in H_{3}(W_{p};\mathbb{K})
(by considering its class in the Grothendieck group of
\mathcal{F}(W_{p};\mathbb{K})
and taking the open-closed map). Picking the correct orientation on
L
, we can assume its homology class in
H_{3}(W_{p};\mathbb{Z})
differs from
(1,0)\in\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}
by something
p
-divisible, hence has the form
(1+d.p,e.p)
for some
d,e\in\mathbb{Z}
.

(2)

HF(L,T_{x}^{*};\mathbb{K})=\mathbb{K}
and
HF(L,T_{y}^{*};\mathbb{K})=0
, where
T_{x}^{*}
is the cotangent fibre to the first core component and
T_{y}^{*}
is the cotangent fibre to the second core component.

Working with Floer cohomology over
\mathbb{Z}
, Euler characteristic with a fixed object (here, the cotangent fibre)

\chi(HF(T_{x}^{*},-;\mathbb{Z})):\{\mathrm{Exact\,closed\,Lagrangians}\}\to\mathbb{Z}

defines a map from the set of exact closed Lagrangians in
W_{p}
to
\mathbb{Z}
. (There is no difference between ordinary and wrapped Floer cohomology here since one of the Lagrangians is assumed compact.) The Euler characteristic of
HF
is, up to sign, given by the algebraic intersection number, so we conclude that the function sends
L
to
\pm(1+d.p)
.

If
d>0
we learn that
\operatorname{rk}_{\mathbb{Z}}(HF(L,T_{x}^{*}))\geqslant 1+d.p
. If
d<0
then
\operatorname{rk}_{\mathbb{Z}}(HF(L,T_{x}^{*}))\geqslant|d|p-1>1
(since by hypothesis we are considering the case
p>2
). However, universal coefficients then says in either case that the rank of
HF(L,T_{x}^{*};\mathbb{K})
is
>1
, which violates the second point above; so we conclude that
d=0
. Similarly, considering
\chi(HF(T_{y}^{*},—;\mathbb{Z}))
we conclude
e=0
. Thus, the
\mathbb{Z}
-homology class of the Lagrangian
L
is
(1,0)
.
∎

Corollary 6.18
.

If
p>2
is prime, then any exact graded closed Lagrangian
L\subset W_{p}
satisfies
H^{*}(L;\mathbb{K})=H^{*}(S^{3};\mathbb{K})
if
\pm[L]\in\{(1,0),(0,1)\}\subset H_{3}(W_{p};\mathbb{Z})
, and
H^{*}(L;\mathbb{K})=H^{*}(L(p,1);\mathbb{K})
if
\pm[L]\in\{(1,\pm 1)\}\subset H_{3}(W_{p};\mathbb{Z})
.

As explained in Remark
6.15
, both the previous results rely essentially on our mirror symmetry statements in
finite
characteristic.

Corollary 6.19
.

If
p=1
or
p>2
is prime, there is no exact Lagrangian
S^{1}\times S^{2}\subset W_{p}
with vanishing Maslov class.

Proof.

Although the graded rings
H^{*}(L(p,1);\mathbb{Z}/p)
and
H^{*}(S^{1}\times S^{2};\mathbb{Z}/p)
agree, the former has a non-trivial
\mu^{3}
-operation (Massey product), whilst the latter is formal. Since the
A_{\infty}
-structure in the endomorphism algebra of an exact Lagrangian reproduces the classical structure on cohomology, the result then follows as before. ∎

Note that
W_{0}

does
contain an exact graded Lagrangian
S^{1}\times S^{2}
, namely the surgery of the two core spheres.

6.5.
Proof of
6.6
and
6.7

In this subsection, which is logically independent of the remainder of the paper, we give the full proofs of the two representation theory facts presented in Section
6.2
. Namely, we establish that if two modules for the contraction algebras
\Lambda_{\operatorname{con}}
or
\Upgamma_{\operatorname{con}}
are orthogonal, then one is filtered by a single simple, and furthermore we prove that both
\Lambda_{\operatorname{con}}
and
\Upgamma_{\operatorname{con}}
admit precisely four bricks.

Our method to approach both problems uses Auslander–Reiten (AR) theory.

Lemma 6.20
.

The AR quivers of the contraction algebras
\Lambda_{\operatorname{con}}
and
\Upgamma_{\operatorname{con}}
are illustrated in Figure
2
, where the numbers denote the dimension vectors of the corresponding representation.

\begin{array}[]{ccc}\includegraphics[angle,scale]{AR1.pdf}&\includegraphics[angle,scale]{AR2.pdf}&\includegraphics[angle,scale]{AR3.pdf}\\
\begin{array}[]{c}\Lambda_{\operatorname{con}}\\
{\scriptstyle k\geqslant 1}\end{array}&\begin{array}[]{c}\Upgamma_{\operatorname{con}}\\
{\scriptstyle k=2r-1,\,\,r\geqslant 2}\end{array}&\begin{array}[]{c}\Upgamma_{\operatorname{con}}\\
{\scriptstyle k=2r,\,\,r\geqslant 1}\end{array}\end{array}

Figure 2
.
AR quivers of
\Lambda_{\operatorname{con}}
and
\Upgamma_{\operatorname{con}}
.

In each case, the left and right dotted arrows are identified, and so AR quiver is really drawn on a cylinder.

Proof.

Both
\Lambda_{\operatorname{con}}
and
\Upgamma_{\operatorname{con}}
are Brauer tree algebras of finite representation type. Further,
\Lambda_{\operatorname{con}}
is a symmetric Nakayama algebra. The above AR quivers are well-known, and can be extracted from e.g.
[
22
]
.
∎

Proof of
6.6
.

The proof for
\Lambda_{\operatorname{con}}
and for
\Upgamma_{\operatorname{con}}
is slightly different. For
\Lambda_{\operatorname{con}}
, we claim that if
X
and
Y
are indecomposable
\Lambda_{\operatorname{con}}
-modules which are not simple, then
\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)\neq 0
. This is just clear from the shape of the AR quiver, and the fact that the simples are in the top row. For example, when
k=3
, the blue region in the following knitting calculation:

shows that there is a non-zero homomorphism from the circled representation to every other indecomposable non-simple module. By the highly regular shape of the AR quiver, the calculation for every other non-simple representation is very similar.

Now suppose that
a,b\in\operatorname{mod}\Lambda_{\operatorname{con}}
satisfies
\mathrm{Hom}(a,b)=0
. By above, if
a
contains a non-simple module, then
b
cannot. But then
b=\mathcal{S}_{1}^{\oplus s}\oplus\mathcal{S}_{2}^{\oplus t}
. Since no non-zero module can be orthogonal to both simples, either
b=\mathcal{S}_{1}^{\oplus s}
or
b=\mathcal{S}_{2}^{\oplus t}
. The only other case is when
a
only contains simple modules; for a similar reason either
a=\mathcal{S}_{1}^{\oplus s}
or
a=\mathcal{S}_{2}^{\oplus t}
.

For
\Upgamma_{\operatorname{con}}
, the proof is slightly different. The trick here is that, due to the asymmetry in the quiver,
\mathcal{S}_{2}
injects into almost all modules, and almost all modules surject onto
\mathcal{S}_{2}
. Indeed, the left hand side of the following digram circles all indecomposable modules
X
for which
\mathrm{Hom}(\mathcal{S}_{2},X)=0
, and the right hand side circles all indecomposable modules
Y
for which
\mathrm{Hom}(Y,\mathcal{S}_{2})=0
. We illustrate the case when
k
is odd; the
k
-even case is similar. Both of these calculations can be achieved via knitting (see below for a very similar calculation).

\mathrm{Hom}(\mathcal{S}_{2},X)=0&&\mathrm{Hom}(Y,\mathcal{S}_{2})=0\end{array}

Write
N
for the indecomposable module in the middle of the bottom row, which is circled in both sides above. Now, we are given
a,b
such that
\mathrm{Hom}(a,b)=0
. If
a
has a summand from the complement of the right hand circles,
and

b
has a summand from the complement of the left hand circles, then
a\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{S}_{2}\hookrightarrow b
, which is a non-zero homomorphism. Hence we can assume that either
a=\mathcal{S}_{1}^{\oplus s}\oplus M_{1}^{\oplus t}\oplus N^{\oplus u}
or
b=\mathcal{S}_{1}^{\oplus s}\oplus M_{2}^{\oplus t}\oplus N^{\oplus u}
.

Now, observe that, for any
x\in\operatorname{mod}\Upgamma_{\operatorname{con}}
,

(by positions in AR quiver)

\displaystyle\mathrm{Hom}(M_{1},x)=0

\displaystyle\iff\mathrm{Hom}(N,x)=0

(
\Upgamma_{\operatorname{con}}
is 0-CY, and
N
is projective)

\displaystyle\iff\mathrm{Hom}(x,N)=0

(by positions in the AR quiver)

\displaystyle\iff\mathrm{Hom}(x,M_{2})=0,

and furthermore the following knitting calculation (illustrated for
k=5
) shows that the first condition, and hence all conditions, is equivalent to
x
being filtered by
\mathcal{S}_{2}
.

In the right hand side of the above, we have circled the modules
x
for which
\mathrm{Hom}(M_{1},x)=0
. By inspection of the dimension vectors in the AR quiver in Figure
2
, the circled modules are precisely those modules filtered by
\mathcal{S}_{2}
.

In the case that
a=\mathcal{S}_{1}^{\oplus s}\oplus M_{1}^{\oplus t}\oplus N^{\oplus u}
, it follows from the proceeding paragraph that if either
u\geqslant 1
or
t\geqslant 1
, then
b
is filtered by
\mathcal{S}_{2}
. Hence we can assume that
u=t=0
, in which case
a=\mathcal{S}_{1}^{\oplus s}
, and so
a
is filtered by
\mathcal{S}_{1}
.

In the case that
b=\mathcal{S}_{1}^{\oplus s}\oplus M_{2}^{\oplus t}\oplus N^{\oplus u}
, in a very similar way, it follows from the proceeding paragraph that if either
u\geqslant 1
or
t\geqslant 1
, then
a
is filtered by
\mathcal{S}_{2}
. Hence we can assume that
u=t=0
, in which case
b=\mathcal{S}_{1}^{\oplus s}
, and so
b
is filtered by
\mathcal{S}_{1}
.
∎

6.7
.

In all cases, there are precisely four modules with one-dimensional endomorphism ring, which we have circled. By inspection of the AR quivers in Lemma
6.20
, the circled modules are either simple, or have dimension vector
(1,1)
. By uniqueness of the non-split extensions between
\mathcal{S}_{1}
and
\mathcal{S}_{2}
, the result follows.
∎

7.
A realisation question

One can hope that Theorem
1.1
sits in a much wider framework; we briefly sketch this here, and highlight some obstructions and subtleties.

As demonstrated by Theorem
1.1
, it may simply not be feasible to expect mirror symmetry statements for
all
flops without changing the characteristic of the field. In addition to this issue, 3-fold flops have moduli, and on the A-side it is not so clear how continuous parameters can enter into the plumbing of spheres, even if we iterate. As such, following a philosophy that the mirror to the exact form should be some point in complex structure moduli space which is picked out arithmetically, we propose that the existence of the flop equation (
3.1
) defined over
\mathbb{Z}
, not just
\mathbb{C}
, is one of the key features of this paper.

Much more generally, we pose the following ‘realisation question’, which is open on both the algebraic and symplectic sides. In both parts we abuse notation, as above Corollary
2.12
, when describing
A_{\infty}
-structures over fields possibly of prime characteristic.

Question 7.1
.

For the quivers
Q
in Figure
3
, and for those potentials
f
defined over
\mathbb{Z}
for which the Jacobi algebra
J_{f}
is finite dimensional (over some field
\mathbb{K}
), does there exist:

(1)

A
3
-fold flop
g\colon Y\to\operatorname{Spec}R
over
\mathbb{K}
, where
Y
is smooth and defined over
\mathbb{Z}
, such that its contraction algebra is isomorphic to
J_{f}
, and the
A_{\infty}
-structure on the Ext-algebra of the curves is also described by
f
?

(2)

An exact symplectic manifold
W_{f}
with
n=|Q_{0}|
distinguished Lagrangians
L_{1},\ldots,L_{n}
, over which each
L_{i}
is fat-spherical and the
A_{\infty}
-algebra
\bigoplus_{i,j}HF^{*}(L_{i},L_{j})
is described by
f
?

For any given potential

7.1
exist, over the appropriate field
\mathbb{K}
the top horizontal row in the following is an equivalence of categories, and it should extend via Koszul duality to an equivalence in the dotted bottom horizontal row, modulo Remark

.

\mathcal{C}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\{a\mid\mathbf{R}g_{*}a=0

Furthermore, on the B-side, there is a known real simplicial hyperplane arrangement
\mathcal{H}
which induces a faithful group action

\uppi_{\hskip 0.5pt1}\hskip-0.5pt(\mathbb{C}^{n}\backslash\mathcal{H}_{\mathbb{C}})\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Auteq}\mathcal{L}.

When
\mathcal{H}
is an ADE root system,
\uppi_{\hskip 0.5pt1}\hskip-0.5pt(\mathbb{C}^{n}\backslash\mathcal{H}_{\mathbb{C}})
is isomorphic to the pure braid group, but in general
\mathcal{H}
need not be Coxeter, and further higher length braid relations exist.

Question
7.1
is very subtle, even for
A_{2}
and
A_{3}
. Most notably, on the B-side the dual graph changes under flop, and so the families in Figure
3
can be related via mutation. More plainly, adding loops to the oriented two-cycle results in
much
more complicated geometry than considered in this paper.
